def scopus_abstract(
    ids,
    by: str = "doi",
    view: str = "META_ABS",
    include: tuple[str, ...] = (),
    cache_dir: str | None = None,
    resume: bool = True,
    **kwargs,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Retrieve abstracts for one or many ids, resilient per id.

    ``ids`` is one identifier, or a list, tuple or pandas Series of them.
    They are checked before any request, as in the R twin. A missing or blank
    identifier raises ``ValueError`` naming its position, counting from 0.
    :func:`scopusflow.corpus.corpus` drops such records itself. Surrounding
    whitespace is trimmed, the ``SCOPUS_ID:`` prefix is dropped when
    ``by="scopus_id"``, and whole numbers are sent as text. Any other value,
    a float or bytes among them, raises ``TypeError``.

    ``by`` selects the lookup type ("doi", "eid" or "scopus_id"). Any id that
    fails is warned about and yields an all-NA row that still records the id.
    ``view`` defaults to "META_ABS" (pybliometrics' own default), which
    carries the abstract text; the lighter "META" omits it and leaves the
    ``abstract`` column empty. ``include``, when unused, leaves the column
    set exactly as before.

    ``include`` names extra fields to retrieve in the same request: any of
    "references", "keywords" (the author keywords) and "index_terms" (the
    index keywords Scopus assigns). "references" needs Abstract Retrieval's
    "FULL" or "REF" view, and "keywords" needs the "FULL" view, since the
    other views carry no author keywords. "index_terms" needs "FULL" as well.
    Any other combination raises ``ValueError`` before a request. Both views
    are an entitlement separate from ordinary abstract access and from Scopus
    Search access. Per
    Elsevier's own documentation, some fields (notably author keywords) may
    need to be requested from your Scopus/Elsevier account contact even when
    the view itself is otherwise accessible. "FULL" returns the whole bibliography in
    one request. "REF" serves it about 40 references per request, and
    pybliometrics pages REF itself, following the view's ``startref``
    parameter until the list is complete, so a document with N references
    costs ``ceil(N / 40)`` requests under "REF". "FULL" is therefore the
    cheaper view when your entitlement allows it. A mismatch between the
    number of references returned and the document's own reported reference
    count (``refcount``) is warned about, since the list may then be
    incomplete.

    When "keywords" is included, an ``authkeywords`` column is added: the
    document's author-supplied keywords, joined with "; ", or ``NA`` when the
    document has none, or when the API omits the field for a given key's
    entitlement. In this package's own development testing, against a live,
    otherwise fully-entitled key, this field did not populate for documents
    that do carry author keywords in Scopus itself, so an all-``NA`` column
    is more likely an entitlement gap worth raising with your Scopus/Elsevier
    account contact than genuinely absent data. A keyword entry that
    pybliometrics cannot parse (its 4.4.1 release raises ``KeyError`` on an
    entry without text) leaves that document's keywords ``NA`` with a
    warning, and the rest of its row is kept.

    When "index_terms" is included, an ``idxterms`` column is added after any
    ``authkeywords``: the document's index keywords, read from
    pybliometrics' ``idxterms`` and joined with "; ", or ``NA`` when the
    response carries none. Authors choose their own keywords, whereas Scopus
    chooses the index keywords and standardises them to vocabularies derived
    from thesauri Elsevier owns or licenses, with synonyms, spellings and
    plurals brought together. The two kinds therefore give different keyword
    co-occurrence results, and a study should say which it used. Elsevier's
    guide lists index keywords in the "FULL" view as not available by
    default, so whether they arrive depends on the key's entitlement as well.
    In this package's development testing, they did arrive on the same key
    whose author keywords came back empty. An index term pybliometrics cannot
    parse (its 4.4.1 release raises ``KeyError`` on one without text) leaves
    that document's index keywords ``NA`` with a warning, and the rest of its
    row is kept. The R twin drops such a term and keeps the others.

    When "references" is included, a ``references`` column is added: one
    DataFrame per document (one row per cited work), using pybliometrics' own
    native field set (``position``, ``id``, ``doi``, ``title``, ``authors``,
    ``authors_auid``, ``authors_affiliationid``, ``sourcetitle``,
    ``publicationyear``, ``coverDate``, ``volume``, ``issue``, ``first``,
    ``last``, ``citedbycount``, ``type``, ``text``, ``fulltext``). A document
    with no resolvable references yields a zero-row DataFrame, so
    the column can always be unnested.

    ``cache_dir`` and ``resume`` checkpoint per identifier, the way
    :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan` checkpoints per cell, pickled rather
    than written as parquet/csv, since a row here can carry a nested
    DataFrame. Only a successful retrieval is checkpointed: a failed
    identifier still yields its warned-about NA row in the returned frame,
    but is retried on the next resumed run, never read back as data.
    Worth setting whenever ``include`` is used: Abstract Retrieval
    draws on its own weekly quota, smaller than and separate from Search's,
    and every identifier costs its own request, so re-running an interrupted
    batch without a cache re-spends quota already spent. A ``cache_dir`` that
    cannot be written raises ``ValueError`` before any request, and a
    checkpoint that cannot be written all the same is warned about, the row
    kept in the result, as in :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan`. Relying on
    pybliometrics' own on-disk response cache (its ``refresh`` parameter,
    keyed by identifier and view under its configured cache directory) is
    enough to avoid repeat network calls for the *same* identifier across
    script runs; this checkpoint is for batch-level progress and resumability
    across *many* identifiers, a separate concern.

    The number of Abstract Retrieval requests made, and the most recently
    parsed remaining-quota figure (from pybliometrics'
    ``get_key_remaining_quota()``), are attached as ``result.attrs["n_requests"]``
    and ``result.attrs["quota"]``, since this is a materially more expensive
    operation than a search call. ``n_requests`` counts each document once,
    however many REF pages pybliometrics requested for it, so it is a count
    of documents fetched. A failed retrieval counts once, since the API has
    usually answered it with an error. A row read from a ``cache_dir``
    checkpoint sent no request and is not counted. Nor is a row pybliometrics
    answered from its own cache, recognised by a cache file older than the
    call or by a response with no headers kept. Such a row's ``citations``
    and other fields date from when that cache file was written. Pass
    ``refresh=True`` to fetch every identifier from the API.

    A 403 (an entitlement gate, most often on the requested view or field)
    raises :class:`scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowForbiddenError` and stops
    the batch immediately, naming the view and identifier, where a generic
    failure would leave the caller guessing. Repeating the identical failure
    for every remaining identifier would serve nobody: entitlement is a
    property of the account, so a retry cannot succeed.

    A spent weekly quota stops the requests too, but returns what the batch
    holds, since it usually arrives part-way through. pybliometrics raises
    ``Scopus429Error`` once every configured key has been refused. The rows
    already retrieved are kept, each identifier not retrieved gets an NA row
    that is not checkpointed, and one
    :class:`scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowQuotaWarning` names the
    identifier reached and how many were not retrieved. A checkpoint in
    ``cache_dir`` is still read after the stop.

    Raises :class:`scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowConfigError` before any
    request when ``pybliometrics.init()`` has not been called in the session.
    An identifier served from its checkpoint sends no request, so a batch
    resumed wholly from checkpoints runs without ``init()``.
    """
    if by not in _ID_TYPES:
        raise ValueError("by must be one of 'doi', 'eid', 'scopus_id'.")
    include = tuple(include) if include else ()
    if not set(include) <= _KNOWN_INCLUDE:
        raise ValueError(
            "include must name only 'references', 'keywords' and 'index_terms'."
        )
    if "references" in include and view not in _VIEWS_WITH_REFERENCES:
        raise ValueError('include="references" needs view="FULL" or view="REF".')
    # The REF response carries no author keywords and META/META_ABS none
    # either, so accepting them would only give a silently all-NA column.
    if "keywords" in include and view != "FULL":
        raise ValueError('include="keywords" needs view="FULL".')
    # Index keywords come only with FULL too (Scopus API Guide, V1, p. 29).
    if "index_terms" in include and view != "FULL":
        raise ValueError('include="index_terms" needs view="FULL".')
    id_type = _ID_TYPES[by]
    id_column = "doi" if by == "doi" else "scopus_id"

    ids = _clean_ids(ids, by)

    columns = [
        *ABSTRACT_COLUMNS,
        *(column for name, column in _INCLUDE_COLUMNS.items() if name in include),
    ]

    cache = _writable_cache(cache_dir)

    # Resolve the dependency once: a missing pybliometrics is a setup error and
    # must be raised in its own right, where masquerading as every id failing
    # to retrieve would hide the account-level cause.
    from pybliometrics.scopus import AbstractRetrieval  # lazy; needs a key
    try:
        # A separate, defensive import: pybliometrics.exception is an internal
        # module, outside pybliometrics.scopus's own public surface, so a
        # minimal test double or an unexpected future reorganisation should
        # degrade to generic exception handling below, which stops it breaking
        # every call to this function.
        from pybliometrics.exception import Scopus403Error
    except ImportError:
        class Scopus403Error(Exception):  # never actually raised; see above
            pass
    try:
        # Imported apart from Scopus403Error, so that a module carrying only
        # one of the two still has the other caught.
        from pybliometrics.exception import Scopus429Error
    except ImportError:
        class Scopus429Error(Exception):  # never actually raised; see above
            pass

    n_requests = 0
    quota = None
    rows = []
    # The identifier at which the quota ran out, and how many identifiers were
    # left without a row from the API from then on.
    quota_spent_at = None
    not_retrieved = 0
    for i, ident in enumerate(ids, start=1):
        checkpoint = (
            _find_abstract_checkpoint(cache, view, include, ident)
            if cache is not None else None
        )
        if checkpoint is not None and resume:
            cached = _read_abstract_checkpoint(checkpoint)
            if cached is None:
                warnings.warn(
                    f"The checkpoint {checkpoint} could not be read back, so it "
                    "was discarded and the identifier retrieved again. An "
                    "interrupted run can leave a checkpoint half-written.",
                    UserWarning,
                    stacklevel=2,
                )
            else:
                logger.info("%d/%d: %s loaded from cache.", i, len(ids), ident)
                rows.append(cached)
                continue

        if quota_spent_at is not None:
            # No request after the quota ran out. Checkpoints above are still
            # read, since they cost nothing, and the NA row is not
            # checkpointed, so a run after the reset retrieves the identifier.
            not_retrieved += 1
            rows.append(_na_row(columns, id_column, ident, include))
            continue

        logger.info("Retrieving %d/%d: %s", i, len(ids), ident)
        # Checked before the first request, outside the per-identifier handler
        # below: an uninitialised pybliometrics would fail every identifier in
        # turn, each failure warned about as if that identifier alone were at
        # fault. An identifier served from its checkpoint sends no request, so
        # a batch resumed wholly from checkpoints needs no init().
        require_init()
        # Each identifier adds to n_requests exactly once, and only when a
        # request went out. A step that fails after the response arrived used
        # to add a second count for the same request. A failed construction
        # counts as one: the API has usually answered it with an error.
        ab = None
        t0 = time.time()
        try:
            ab = AbstractRetrieval(ident, id_type=id_type, view=view, **kwargs)
            if _served_from_cache(ab, t0, kwargs.get("refresh", False)):
                logger.info("%d/%d: %s read from pybliometrics' cache.", i, len(ids), ident)
            else:
                n_requests += 1
            # Optional: an object without these methods (a plain dict, or a
            # minimal stand-in) simply reports no quota, and does not fail
            # the whole retrieval over a metadata nicety. Both lookups are
            # guarded, since an object carrying only the first would otherwise
            # fail here after a successful retrieval and record an NA row.
            get_quota = getattr(ab, "get_key_remaining_quota", None)
            get_reset = getattr(ab, "get_key_reset_time", None)
            remaining = get_quota() if callable(get_quota) else None
            if remaining is not None:
                reset = get_reset() if callable(get_reset) else None
                quota = {"remaining": remaining, "reset": reset}
            row = _abstract_row(ab, include=include, ident=ident)
        except Scopus403Error as exc:
            n_requests += 1
            remaining_ids = len(ids) - i
            # The FULL/REF alternative is only sensible advice when the failed
            # view was one of the two reference-carrying views; a 403 on a
            # plain META/META_ABS retrieval is an ordinary entitlement gap.
            alternative = (
                ' or, if you have not already, try the other of "FULL"/"REF"'
                if view in _VIEWS_WITH_REFERENCES else ""
            )
            raise ScopusFlowForbiddenError(
                f'Abstract Retrieval refused view="{view}" (HTTP 403) for {ident!r}. '
                "This usually means your Scopus API key's entitlement does not cover "
                "the requested view or field; contact your Scopus/Elsevier account "
                f"holder or institutional administrator to request access{alternative}. "
                "Stopping rather "
                f"than repeating the same failure for the remaining {remaining_ids} "
                "identifier(s) (this entitlement is an account-level property, not a "
                "per-document one, so it will not succeed on retry)."
            ) from exc
        except Scopus429Error:
            # pybliometrics raises this only once every configured key has
            # been refused, and documents it as a depleted weekly quota, so no
            # later identifier could succeed until the reset. The batch stops
            # requesting but keeps its rows: unlike a 403, a spent quota
            # usually arrives part-way through, and raising would discard the
            # rows already paid for when cache_dir is not set.
            if ab is None:
                n_requests += 1
            quota_spent_at = ident
            not_retrieved += 1
            rows.append(_na_row(columns, id_column, ident, include))
            continue
        except Exception:  # one bad id must not sink the batch
            if ab is None:  # a response that arrived was counted above
                n_requests += 1
            warnings.warn(
                f"Could not retrieve abstract for {ident!r}; recording NA row.",
                stacklevel=2,
            )
            # Never checkpointed: a timeout or a 5xx may pass, and a persisted
            # NA row would be read back as data on every later resume. The
            # identifier is retried instead, at the cost of one request.
            rows.append(_na_row(columns, id_column, ident, include))
            continue

        if cache is not None:
            # A failed write keeps the row its request paid for, as a cell's
            # does in fetch_plan().
            try:
                _write_abstract_checkpoint(row, cache, view, include, ident)
            except OSError:
                warnings.warn(
                    _unwritable_warning(repr(ident), cache, "its record is"),
                    stacklevel=2,
                )
        rows.append(row)

    if quota_spent_at is not None:
        warnings.warn(
            _quota_warning(quota_spent_at, not_retrieved, quota),
            ScopusFlowQuotaWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=columns)
    out.attrs["n_requests"] = n_requests
    out.attrs["quota"] = quota
    return out

corpus(records, by='doi', view='FULL', cache_dir=None, resume=True, keywords='author', **kwargs)

Enrich records (from :func:scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan) with keywords (the author keywords by default, or the index keywords Scopus assigns) and structured references via Abstract Retrieval, returning a minimal, uniform shape close to what OpenAlex's works API already returns: id, scopus_id, title, year, keywords (a list of strings per row) and references (a DataFrame of cited works per row). :func:write_corpus writes the result in theoryforge's corpus schema. This is meant for downstream tools that want to consume Scopus output without writing their own parsing layer, for example for keyword co-occurrence or citation-network analysis. Only the "FULL" view carries author keywords, so under "REF" the references alone are requested and every keywords entry is empty. references carries pybliometrics' own native reference field set (see :func:scopus_abstract's documentation).

def corpus(
    records: pd.DataFrame,
    by: str = "doi",
    view: str = "FULL",
    cache_dir: str | None = None,
    resume: bool = True,
    keywords: str = "author",
    **kwargs,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Enrich ``records`` (from :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan`) with
    keywords (the author keywords by default, or the index keywords Scopus
    assigns) and structured references via Abstract Retrieval, returning a
    minimal, uniform shape close to what OpenAlex's ``works`` API already
    returns: ``id``, ``scopus_id``, ``title``, ``year``, ``keywords`` (a list
    of strings per row) and ``references`` (a DataFrame of cited works per
    row). :func:`write_corpus` writes the result in theoryforge's corpus
    schema. This is meant for downstream tools that want to consume Scopus
    output without writing their own parsing layer, for example for keyword
    co-occurrence or citation-network analysis. It does not replace
    :func:`to_bibtex`/
    :func:`to_ris`, which keep their own established interchange formats.

    ``by`` selects which column of ``records`` ("doi" or "scopus_id") to look
    identifiers up by. ``view`` is passed to :func:`scopus_abstract` and
    defaults to "FULL", which returns a document's whole bibliography in one
    request. "REF" serves it about 40 references per request, and
    pybliometrics pages REF itself, so the list still arrives whole, at a cost
    of ``ceil(N / 40)`` requests for N references (see
    :func:`scopus_abstract`'s documentation for the entitlement each view
    needs). ``cache_dir`` and ``resume`` are passed through unchanged, and are
    worth setting for anything beyond a handful of records, since this
    performs at least one Abstract Retrieval request per record, against its
    own, smaller weekly quota, separate from Search's. What that cost came to
    is carried through from :func:`scopus_abstract`: the number of requests
    made, counting each document once, and the most recently parsed
    remaining-quota figure are attached as ``result.attrs["n_requests"]`` and
    ``result.attrs["quota"]``. Three more ``attrs`` carry what
    :func:`write_corpus` records of the corpus's provenance. ``query`` is a
    list of the field-wrapped search expression of each cell of the records'
    plan, or, for records without a plan, of the distinct values of their own
    ``query`` column. ``retrieved_at`` is when the search that found the
    records ran, as the records hold it, and ``keywords`` is the kind of
    keyword chosen. ``query`` and ``retrieved_at`` are ``None`` when
    ``records`` carries neither.

    ``scopus_id`` is the document's own Scopus identifier, as Abstract
    Retrieval gives it, or the ``scopus_id`` of ``records`` where Abstract
    Retrieval gives none, as for a failed lookup, and missing when neither
    has one.

    A record whose identifier is missing (``NA``/``None``) or blank is
    dropped, with a warning naming how many.

    The `keywords` column here is `list[str]` per row, split out of
    :func:`scopus_abstract`'s joined `authkeywords` and `idxterms` strings,
    empty when the document has none or the field is unavailable. Only the
    "FULL" view carries author keywords, so under "REF" the references alone
    are requested and every `keywords` entry is empty. `references` carries
    pybliometrics' own native reference field set (see
    :func:`scopus_abstract`'s documentation).

    ``keywords`` chooses which keywords fill that column: "author" (the
    default) for the author keywords, "index" for the index keywords Scopus
    assigns, or "both" for the author keywords followed by each index keyword
    not already among them. The match is on the exact text, so a term that
    differs only in case appears twice. "index" and "both" need
    ``view="FULL"``, since the "REF" response carries no keywords of either
    kind, and raise ``ValueError`` under "REF" before any request. Index
    keywords and author keywords give different co-occurrence results, and
    :func:`scopus_abstract` describes how each is chosen and the entitlement
    each depends on. Either choice costs the same request per record.
    """
    if keywords not in _KEYWORD_SOURCES:
        raise ValueError(
            f"keywords must be one of 'author', 'index' or 'both', not {keywords!r}."
        )
    # Checked here, so that the error names this function's own argument, where
    # scopus_abstract() would name the include value it was passed.
    if keywords != "author" and view != "FULL":
        raise ValueError(
            f'keywords="{keywords}" needs view="FULL", since the REF response '
            "carries no index keywords."
        )
    required = {by, "title", "year"}
    if not required.issubset(records.columns):
        raise ValueError(
            f"records must have {sorted(required)} columns "
            "(as fetch_plan() returns)."
        )

    # The search behind the records, read before they are subset: the
    # field-wrapped query each cell sent, as the search record states it, and
    # when the search ran.
    expression = _expression(records, as_plan(records.attrs.get("plan")))
    retrieved_at = records.attrs.get("retrieved_at")

    ids = records[by]
    # Blank text counts as missing too, since scopus_abstract() refuses both.
    keep = ~ids.map(_is_missing_identifier).astype(bool)
    n_dropped = int((~keep).sum())
    if n_dropped:
        warnings.warn(
            f"Dropped {n_dropped} record(s) with no usable {by}.",
            stacklevel=2,
        )
    if not keep.any():
        raise ValueError("records has no usable identifiers to look up.")
    records = records.loc[keep].reset_index(drop=True)

    # The REF response carries no author keywords (scopus_abstract() refuses
    # the combination), so under that view only the references are requested
    # and every record's keywords come back empty, as in the R twin. Under
    # FULL, only the kinds of keyword asked for are included, which keeps the
    # checkpoints of a default corpus named as before.
    include = ("references",)
    if view == "FULL":
        if keywords in ("author", "both"):
            include += ("keywords",)
        if keywords in ("index", "both"):
            include += ("index_terms",)
    ab = scopus_abstract(
        list(records[by]), by=by, view=view, include=include,
        cache_dir=cache_dir, resume=resume, **kwargs,
    )

    def _split(column):
        if column not in ab:
            return [[] for _ in range(len(ab))]
        return [[] if pd.isna(kw) else [k.strip() for k in kw.split(";")]
                for kw in ab[column]]

    author, index = _split("authkeywords"), _split("idxterms")
    if keywords == "author":
        terms = author
    elif keywords == "index":
        terms = index
    else:
        # dict.fromkeys() keeps the first of each repeated text, as R's
        # unique() does, so the author keywords come first and an index
        # keyword they already hold is not repeated.
        terms = [list(dict.fromkeys(a + i)) for a, i in zip(author, index, strict=True)]

    # The document's own identifier, from Abstract Retrieval. A failed lookup
    # leaves it missing there, and the records' own identifier fills the gap
    # where they carry one, as in the R twin.
    scopus_id = [_text(v) for v in ab["scopus_id"]]
    if "scopus_id" in records.columns:
        scopus_id = [s if s is not None else _text(r)
                     for s, r in zip(scopus_id, records["scopus_id"], strict=True)]

    out = pd.DataFrame({
        # The identifier used to look each record up, taken from `records`
        # directly, and never read back from `ab`: scopus_abstract() only
        # echoes the input identifier verbatim in its "doi"/"scopus_id"
        # column on a failed lookup (to keep the failing row identifiable);
        # on success that column holds whatever Scopus itself returns, which
        # is usually but not guaranteedly identical to the input.
        "id": list(records[by]),
        "scopus_id": pd.Series([pd.NA if s is None else s for s in scopus_id], dtype=object),
        "title": records["title"],
        "year": records["year"],
        "keywords": terms,
        "references": list(ab["references"]),
    })
    # A freshly constructed frame carries no attrs, so the wrapper that spends
    # the most quota would otherwise be the one reporting none of it.
    out.attrs.update(ab.attrs)
    # The provenance write_corpus() records, as JSON-safe values: the
    # expressions as a list, the time as the records hold it.
    out.attrs["query"] = expression
    out.attrs["retrieved_at"] = retrieved_at
    out.attrs["keywords"] = keywords
    return out

to_records(results, query=None, view=None, fields='core')

Normalise a pybliometrics ScopusSearch().results list (named tuples) or a list of dicts into a tidy :data:RECORD_COLUMNS DataFrame.

Whatever the query type, the columns are the same, so the downstream DOI, diff and analysis helpers can rely on them.

What authors holds depends on the view. The Search API's dc:creator, pybliometrics' creator, is the first author alone under either view, in the indexed form Scopus uses ("Zhang F."). The author list arrives only under view="COMPLETE", and pybliometrics builds author_names from it as "Surname, Given" names. Those names are joined here with "; ", as the R twin joins them, and an author whose given name is null or empty is written as the surname alone. A row without the list falls back to creator. A STANDARD record therefore names its first author, and :func:top says so once when it tallies a STANDARD harvest by author. The API lists at most 100 authors per record. The R twin builds the same string from the same entry in the common case, and the two part company at two edges. pybliometrics builds author_names only when every author object carries both a surname and a given-name key, so where one does not, this twin keeps the first author while the R twin lists every author. Where a surname is null or empty, pybliometrics writes the given name after a bare comma, and the R twin uses the indexed name.

When view="COMPLETE", an authkeywords column is added: the author- supplied keywords the Scopus Search API returns under that view, as a single string in Scopus's own " | "-delimited form (None when the document has none, or when the API omits the field for a given key's entitlement: this was observed directly against a live, otherwise fully-entitled key during development, on documents that do carry author keywords in Scopus itself, so an all-None column is more likely an entitlement gap worth raising with your Scopus/Elsevier account contact than genuinely absent data). Any other view, including the default None, reproduces :data:RECORD_COLUMNS exactly, so existing callers that never pass view see no change at all.

fields is "core" by default, which builds the columns above exactly as before. "extended" also keeps fields the Search API sends with every record, at no extra quota, which pybliometrics already parses: the :data:EXTENDED_COLUMNS and, under view="COMPLETE", an abstract column. Elsevier's Search views table lists every one of them under both views except the abstract (dc:description), which only COMPLETE carries. A COMPLETE harvest therefore returns up to 25 abstracts with each request, while :func:scopusflow.abstract.scopus_abstract spends one request per record from the separate Abstract Retrieval quota.

doc_type and doc_type_description hold the document-type code and name Scopus gives the record, such as "ar" and "Article". The code is the one the DOCTYPE() search field takes, and Elsevier's search tips list the codes with their names: ar for an article, re a review, cp a conference paper, er an erratum and others. A retracted item carries tb, which that list leaves out. The Scopus Content Coverage Guide (Elsevier, 2023, section 3.1) defines an erratum as a report of an error, correction or retraction of a previously published paper, so er covers retraction notices as well as corrections. The guide gives an article the type Retracted once a retraction notice for it is published. These codes are the labels Scopus assigns, and they do not screen a set for retractions, since Scopus does not label every retracted item (Ortega and Delgado-Quirós, 2024, Scientometrics, 129(7), 3769-3785). Check a set against the Retraction Watch database, which Crossref makes openly available, before relying on it. Errata can also be left out of the search itself with AND NOT DOCTYPE(er), joined by :func:scopusflow.query.scopus_query, which brackets the rest of the query first, since Scopus applies AND NOT last.

source_type holds the source type, such as "Journal". volume, issue, pages and pubmed_id are text, and so is issn, the print ISSN as Scopus writes it, without the hyphen, so its leading zeros survive. open_access holds the code Scopus sends in its openaccess field, as a whole number. Elsevier's Scopus APIs Getting Started Guide (2023, section 17) illustrates its values with 0 for a record that is not open access, 1 for gold and 2 for green. The column therefore holds a status code, which can take values other than 0 and 1. A fields value other than "core" or "extended" raises ValueError.

def to_records(
    results, query: str | None = None, view: str | None = None, fields: str = "core"
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Normalise a pybliometrics ``ScopusSearch().results`` list (named tuples)
    or a list of dicts into a tidy :data:`RECORD_COLUMNS` DataFrame.

    Whatever the query type, the columns are the same, so the downstream DOI,
    diff and analysis helpers can rely on them.

    What ``authors`` holds depends on the view. The Search API's
    ``dc:creator``, pybliometrics' ``creator``, is the first author alone under
    either view, in the indexed form Scopus uses (``"Zhang F."``). The author
    list arrives only under ``view="COMPLETE"``, and pybliometrics builds
    ``author_names`` from it as ``"Surname, Given"`` names. Those names are
    joined here with ``"; "``, as the R twin joins them, and an author whose
    given name is null or empty is written as the surname alone. A row without
    the list falls back to ``creator``. A ``STANDARD`` record therefore names
    its first author, and :func:`top` says so once when it tallies a
    ``STANDARD`` harvest by author. The API lists at most 100 authors per
    record. The R twin builds the same string from the same entry in the common
    case, and the two part company at two edges. pybliometrics builds
    ``author_names`` only when every author object carries both a ``surname``
    and a ``given-name`` key, so where one does not, this twin keeps the first
    author while the R twin lists every author. Where a surname is null or
    empty, pybliometrics writes the given name after a bare comma, and the R
    twin uses the indexed name.

    When ``view="COMPLETE"``, an ``authkeywords`` column is added: the author-
    supplied keywords the Scopus Search API returns under that view, as a
    single string in Scopus's own ``" | "``-delimited form (``None`` when the
    document has none, or when the API omits the field for a given key's
    entitlement: this was observed directly against a live, otherwise
    fully-entitled key during development, on documents that do carry author
    keywords in Scopus itself, so an all-``None`` column is more likely an
    entitlement gap worth raising with your Scopus/Elsevier account contact
    than genuinely absent data). Any other ``view``, including the default
    ``None``, reproduces :data:`RECORD_COLUMNS` exactly, so existing callers
    that never pass ``view`` see no change at all.

    ``fields`` is ``"core"`` by default, which builds the columns above exactly
    as before. ``"extended"`` also keeps fields the Search API sends with every
    record, at no extra quota, which pybliometrics already parses: the
    :data:`EXTENDED_COLUMNS` and, under ``view="COMPLETE"``, an ``abstract``
    column. Elsevier's Search views table lists every one of them under both
    views except the abstract (``dc:description``), which only ``COMPLETE``
    carries. A ``COMPLETE`` harvest therefore returns up to 25 abstracts with
    each request, while :func:`scopusflow.abstract.scopus_abstract` spends one
    request per record from the separate Abstract Retrieval quota.

    ``doc_type`` and ``doc_type_description`` hold the document-type code and
    name Scopus gives the record, such as ``"ar"`` and ``"Article"``. The code
    is the one the ``DOCTYPE()`` search field takes, and Elsevier's search tips
    list the codes with their names: ``ar`` for an article, ``re`` a review,
    ``cp`` a conference paper, ``er`` an erratum and others. A retracted item
    carries ``tb``, which that list leaves out. The Scopus Content Coverage
    Guide (Elsevier, 2023, section 3.1) defines an erratum as a report of an
    error, correction or retraction of a previously published paper, so ``er``
    covers retraction notices as well as corrections. The guide gives an
    article the type Retracted once a retraction notice for it is published.
    These codes are the labels Scopus assigns, and they do not screen a set for
    retractions, since Scopus does not label every retracted item (Ortega and
    Delgado-Quirós, 2024, Scientometrics, 129(7), 3769-3785). Check a set
    against the Retraction Watch database, which Crossref makes openly
    available, before relying on it. Errata can also be left out of the search
    itself with ``AND NOT DOCTYPE(er)``, joined by
    :func:`scopusflow.query.scopus_query`, which brackets the rest of the
    query first, since Scopus applies AND NOT last.

    ``source_type`` holds the source type, such as ``"Journal"``. ``volume``,
    ``issue``, ``pages`` and ``pubmed_id`` are text, and so is ``issn``, the
    print ISSN as Scopus writes it, without the hyphen, so its leading zeros
    survive. ``open_access`` holds the code Scopus sends in its ``openaccess``
    field, as a whole number. Elsevier's Scopus APIs Getting Started Guide
    (2023, section 17) illustrates its values with 0 for a record that is not
    open access, 1 for gold and 2 for green. The column therefore holds a
    status code, which can take values other than 0 and 1. A ``fields`` value
    other than ``"core"`` or ``"extended"`` raises ``ValueError``.
    """
    _check_fields(fields)
    add_keywords = view == "COMPLETE"
    extended = fields == "extended"
    columns = _record_columns(view, fields)
    rows = []
    for i, r in enumerate(results or [], start=1):
        date = _get(r, "coverDate")
        row = {
            "entry_number": i,
            "scopus_id": _scopus_id(_get(r, "eid")),
            "doi": _get(r, "doi"),
            "title": _get(r, "title"),
            # author_names exists only under COMPLETE, and creator is the first author.
            "authors": _join_authors(_get(r, "author_names")) or _get(r, "creator"),
            "year": _year(date),
            "date": date,
            "publication": _get(r, "publicationName"),
            "citations": _citations(_get(r, "citedby_count")),
            "query": query,
        }
        if add_keywords:
            row["authkeywords"] = _get(r, "authkeywords") or pd.NA
        if extended:
            for column, source in _EXTENDED_SOURCES.items():
                row[column] = _get(r, source)
            row["open_access"] = _open_access(_get(r, "openaccess"))
            if add_keywords:
                row["abstract"] = _get(r, "description")
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=columns)

docs.text:
top(records, by='source', n=10)

Tally the most frequent sources or authors in a record set.

Author strings holding several names are split on ";", so each contributor is counted once per record. Only a view="COMPLETE" harvest holds several names, since STANDARD records carry the first author alone (see :func:to_records). A tally by author of a harvest whose attrs["view"] is "STANDARD" therefore counts first authorships, and says so with a UserWarning, once per process, in the R twin's words.

Each value is stripped of the white space R's trimws() removes, which is spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds. A value left empty is dropped, as is a missing one, so a blank source title is not counted as a journal.

The result has the columns value and n. It is sorted by descending count, with ties broken by value in code-point order. For UTF-8 text that is the byte order the R twin's scopus_top() sorts by, in which capitals come before lower case. The first n rows are returned, or every row when there are fewer distinct values. Where several values tie at the cut-off, the ones that sort first are kept, the same ones on every machine and in both twins, whatever the order of the records.

n must be one positive whole number. A whole float such as 5.0 and a numpy integer are taken, as the R twin takes any finite whole number, and an n beyond the number of distinct values returns them all. A bool, NaN, infinity, a fraction or a value below 1 raises ValueError, as does a by other than "source" or "author".

def top(records: pd.DataFrame, by: str = "source", n: int = 10) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Tally the most frequent sources or authors in a record set.

    Author strings holding several names are split on ``";"``, so each
    contributor is counted once per record. Only a ``view="COMPLETE"`` harvest
    holds several names, since ``STANDARD`` records carry the first author alone
    (see :func:`to_records`). A tally by author of a harvest whose
    ``attrs["view"]`` is ``"STANDARD"`` therefore counts first authorships, and
    says so with a ``UserWarning``, once per process, in the R twin's words.

    Each value is stripped of the white space R's ``trimws()`` removes, which is
    spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds. A value left empty is dropped,
    as is a missing one, so a blank source title is not counted as a journal.

    The result has the columns ``value`` and ``n``. It is sorted by descending
    count, with ties broken by ``value`` in code-point order. For UTF-8 text that
    is the byte order the R twin's ``scopus_top()`` sorts by, in which capitals
    come before lower case. The first ``n`` rows are returned, or every row when
    there are fewer distinct values. Where several values tie at the cut-off,
    the ones that sort first are kept, the same ones on every machine and in
    both twins, whatever the order of the records.

    ``n`` must be one positive whole number. A whole float such as ``5.0`` and a
    numpy integer are taken, as the R twin takes any finite whole number, and an
    ``n`` beyond the number of distinct values returns them all. A bool, NaN,
    infinity, a fraction or a value below 1 raises ``ValueError``, as does a
    ``by`` other than ``"source"`` or ``"author"``.
    """
    if by not in ("source", "author"):
        raise ValueError("by must be 'source' or 'author'.")
    n = _top_n(n)
    if by == "source":
        values = [str(value) for value in records["publication"].dropna()]
    else:
        _warn_first_author_only(records)
        values = [name for joined in records["authors"].dropna()
                  for name in str(joined).split(";")]
    # Python's own str methods throughout, since pandas 3 hands a text column's
    # .str methods to Arrow, and an object column sorts by Python's comparison,
    # which is code-point order under every pandas version and storage.
    values = [value.strip(_R_WHITESPACE) for value in values]
    tally = (
        pd.Series([value for value in values if value], dtype=object)
        .value_counts()
        .rename_axis("value")
        .reset_index(name="n")
    )
    # value_counts() orders the counts with an unstable sort, so its order among
    # tied values followed the row order and numpy's sort implementation. Each
    # value appears once in the tally, so count and value together order every
    # row, and the R twin orders its rows on the same two keys.
    tally = tally.sort_values(["n", "value"], ascending=[False, True])
    return tally.head(n).reset_index(drop=True)

scopus_combine(*sets, dedupe=False)

Bind several record frames into one, renumbering entry_number.

This is the safe way to merge separate harvests: a plain concat leaves duplicate entry numbers, and nothing then records how many records went in.

De-duplication compares DOIs as :func:scopusflow.diff.extract_dois does, without resolver prefixes such as https://doi.org/ or doi: and ignoring case. It keeps the first record of each group, in the order the sets were given, and a record with neither an identifier nor a DOI cannot be matched and is kept.

Under the default rule, records with the same Scopus identifier are one record, and a record without an identifier joins the identified record that carries its DOI. Records with different identifiers are never merged, even when they share a DOI. Scopus holds duplicate records of one paper (Valderrama-Zurián et al., 2015), but it also gives one DOI to distinct papers (Franceschini et al., 2015), and a review loses a wrongly removed record for good where a surviving duplicate is caught at screening. Such DOIs are counted in doi_conflicts, which the search record reports, so that they can be checked by hand. A record without an identifier whose DOI two identified records carry is kept once, apart from both. Records without an identifier that share a DOI no identified record carries are one record.

"id_or_doi" merges every record linked to another by a shared identifier or a shared DOI, directly or through a chain of such links. It suits a set whose shared DOIs have been checked and found to be duplicates. "id_then_doi" keys each record on its identifier, failing that on its DOI lower-cased but not otherwise cleaned, and so reproduces a set de-duplicated by scopusflow 0.4.0 or earlier.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *sets

Two or more record frames, or a single list of them.

() dedupe bool | str

Whether, and by which rule, to keep once the records that are one record. False, the default, keeps every row. True, also spelled "id_or_shared_doi", treats records as one when they share a Scopus identifier, or when they share a DOI and one of them lacks an identifier. "id_or_doi" also merges records with different identifiers that share a DOI, and "id_then_doi" applies the rule of scopusflow 0.4.0 and earlier.

False

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

The merged records. Attributes describing a single retrieval, among them plan, total_results and cell_totals, are not carried over, since a set built from several harvests is none of them. Five survive a merge, each only when every input carries it. retrieved_at is the earliest of the inputs' times, retrieved_until the latest (an input without one counting by its retrieved_at) and scopusflow_version a sorted list of every contributing version, while paging and view are kept only where the inputs agree on them. The search record of a merged set is then dated from its first retrieval to its last, as the R twin's is. The merge itself is recorded in attrs["combined"], a dict of n_in (records supplied), n_out (records kept), n_removed, deduplicated, rule (the rule applied, None when none was) and doi_conflicts (how many DOIs records with different identifiers share, None when no rule was applied). That count exists only at the moment of the merge, and PRISMA-S asks for it (item 16), so :func:scopusflow.report.scopus_search_report reads it back from there and states how many duplicates were removed and how.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

When dedupe is neither a bool nor the name of a rule, or an input is not a record frame.

References

Franceschini, F., Maisano, D., & Mastrogiacomo, L. (2015). Errors in DOI indexing by bibliometric databases. Scientometrics, 102(3), 2181–2186. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-014-1503-4

Valderrama-Zurián, J.-C., Aguilar-Moya, R., Melero-Fuentes, D., & Aleixandre-Benavent, R. (2015). A systematic analysis of duplicate records in Scopus. Journal of Informetrics, 9(3), 570–576. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2015.05.002

>>> baseline = sf.example_records()
>>> later = sf.example_records()
>>> merged = sf.scopus_combine(baseline, later, dedupe=True)
>>> merged.attrs["combined"]["n_in"]

>>> len(merged)

def scopus_combine(*sets, dedupe: bool | str = False) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Bind several record frames into one, renumbering ``entry_number``.

    This is the safe way to merge separate harvests: a plain ``concat`` leaves
    duplicate entry numbers, and nothing then records how many records went in.

    De-duplication compares DOIs as :func:`scopusflow.diff.extract_dois` does,
    without resolver prefixes such as ``https://doi.org/`` or ``doi:`` and
    ignoring case. It keeps the first record of each group, in the order the
    sets were given, and a record with neither an identifier nor a DOI cannot
    be matched and is kept.

    Under the default rule, records with the same Scopus identifier are one
    record, and a record without an identifier joins the identified record
    that carries its DOI. Records with different identifiers are never merged,
    even when they share a DOI. Scopus holds duplicate records of one paper
    (Valderrama-Zurián et al., 2015), but it also gives one DOI to distinct
    papers (Franceschini et al., 2015), and a review loses a wrongly removed
    record for good where a surviving duplicate is caught at screening. Such
    DOIs are counted in ``doi_conflicts``, which the search record reports, so
    that they can be checked by hand. A record without an identifier whose DOI
    two identified records carry is kept once, apart from both. Records without
    an identifier that share a DOI no identified record carries are one record.

    ``"id_or_doi"`` merges every record linked to another by a shared
    identifier or a shared DOI, directly or through a chain of such links. It
    suits a set whose shared DOIs have been checked and found to be
    duplicates. ``"id_then_doi"`` keys each record on its identifier, failing
    that on its DOI lower-cased but not otherwise cleaned, and so reproduces a
    set de-duplicated by scopusflow 0.4.0 or earlier.

    Parameters
    ----------
    *sets:
        Two or more record frames, or a single list of them.
    dedupe:
        Whether, and by which rule, to keep once the records that are one
        record. ``False``, the default, keeps every row. ``True``, also spelled
        ``"id_or_shared_doi"``, treats records as one when they share a Scopus
        identifier, or when they share a DOI and one of them lacks an
        identifier. ``"id_or_doi"`` also merges records with different
        identifiers that share a DOI, and ``"id_then_doi"`` applies the rule of
        scopusflow 0.4.0 and earlier.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        The merged records. Attributes describing a single retrieval, among
        them ``plan``, ``total_results`` and ``cell_totals``, are not carried
        over, since a set built from several harvests is none of them. Five
        survive a merge, each only when every input carries it.
        ``retrieved_at`` is the earliest of the inputs' times,
        ``retrieved_until`` the latest (an input without one counting by its
        ``retrieved_at``) and ``scopusflow_version`` a sorted list of every
        contributing version, while ``paging`` and ``view`` are kept only where
        the inputs agree on them. The search record of a merged set is then
        dated from its first retrieval to its last, as the R twin's is. The
        merge itself is recorded in ``attrs["combined"]``, a dict of ``n_in``
        (records supplied), ``n_out`` (records kept), ``n_removed``,
        ``deduplicated``, ``rule`` (the rule applied, ``None`` when none was)
        and ``doi_conflicts`` (how many DOIs records with different
        identifiers share, ``None`` when no rule was applied). That count
        exists only at the moment of the merge, and PRISMA-S asks for it (item
        16), so :func:`scopusflow.report.scopus_search_report` reads it back
        from there and states how many duplicates were removed and how.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        When ``dedupe`` is neither a bool nor the name of a rule, or an input
        is not a record frame.

    References
    ----------
    Franceschini, F., Maisano, D., & Mastrogiacomo, L. (2015). Errors in DOI
    indexing by bibliometric databases. *Scientometrics*, *102*(3), 2181–2186.
    https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-014-1503-4

    Valderrama-Zurián, J.-C., Aguilar-Moya, R., Melero-Fuentes, D., &
    Aleixandre-Benavent, R. (2015). A systematic analysis of duplicate records
    in Scopus. *Journal of Informetrics*, *9*(3), 570–576.
    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2015.05.002

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import scopusflow as sf
    >>> baseline = sf.example_records()
    >>> later = sf.example_records()
    >>> merged = sf.scopus_combine(baseline, later, dedupe=True)
    >>> merged.attrs["combined"]["n_in"]
    276
    >>> len(merged)
    149
    """
    rule = _rule(dedupe)
    frames = list(sets)
    if len(frames) == 1 and isinstance(frames[0], (list, tuple)):
        frames = list(frames[0])
    if not frames or not all(isinstance(f, pd.DataFrame) for f in frames):
        raise ValueError("All inputs to scopus_combine() must be record frames.")

    out = pd.concat([_without_attrs(f) for f in frames], ignore_index=True)
    n_in = len(out)
    conflicts = None
    if rule is not None:
        keys, conflicts = _record_groups(out, rule)
        out = out[~pd.Series(keys, dtype=object).duplicated().to_numpy()].reset_index(
            drop=True)
    if len(out):
        out["entry_number"] = range(1, len(out) + 1)
    else:
        out = out.reindex(columns=list(out.columns) or list(RECORD_COLUMNS))
    # The rule is recorded beside the counts, since the search record has to
    # say how records were matched, and a set merged by 0.4.0 records none.
    out.attrs["combined"] = {
        "n_in": n_in,
        "n_out": len(out),
        "n_removed": n_in - len(out),
        "deduplicated": rule is not None,
        "rule": rule,
        "doi_conflicts": conflicts,
    }
    _bind_provenance(out, frames)
    return out

write_records(records, path)

Save a record set, choosing the format from the file extension.

A .parquet file keeps the provenance in records.attrs: the plan, the retrieval time, the per-cell totals, the paging mode, the software version and any merge record, all of which :func:scopusflow.report.scopus_search_report reads back. They are stored as a JSON block under the scopusflow key of the file's schema metadata, so they survive whatever the pandas version. pandas 1.5 to 2.0 drop attrs when writing parquet, and later versions keep them under a key of their own. Attributes set by hand as a SearchPlan, a datetime or a DataFrame are written in the JSON forms :func:scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan uses, and the frame passed in is left as it was. Parquet needs pyarrow, which the parquet extra installs.

A .csv file is portable plain text, written with LF line endings on every platform, and holds the columns only. Save a baseline you will compare against later as parquet, so that it keeps the record of how it was retrieved.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default records DataFrame

A record frame, such as :func:scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan returns.

required path

The file to write, ending in .parquet or .csv. It is written at exactly this path, and its directory must already exist.

required

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

records, unchanged.

Examples:

>>> import tempfile, pathlib
>>> import scopusflow as sf
>>> path = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "baseline.csv"
>>> _ = sf.write_records(sf.example_records(), path)
>>> len(sf.read_records(path))

def write_records(records: pd.DataFrame, path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Save a record set, choosing the format from the file extension.

    A ``.parquet`` file keeps the provenance in ``records.attrs``: the plan,
    the retrieval time, the per-cell totals, the paging mode, the software
    version and any merge record, all of which
    :func:`scopusflow.report.scopus_search_report` reads back. They are stored
    as a JSON block under the ``scopusflow`` key of the file's schema
    metadata, so they survive whatever the pandas version. pandas 1.5 to 2.0
    drop ``attrs`` when writing parquet, and later versions keep them under a
    key of their own. Attributes set by hand as a ``SearchPlan``, a
    ``datetime`` or a DataFrame are written in the JSON forms
    :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan` uses, and the frame passed in is left
    as it was. Parquet needs pyarrow, which the ``parquet`` extra installs.

    A ``.csv`` file is portable plain text, written with LF line endings on
    every platform, and holds the columns only. Save a baseline you will
    compare against later as parquet, so that it keeps the record of how it
    was retrieved.

    Parameters
    ----------
    records:
        A record frame, such as :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan` returns.
    path:
        The file to write, ending in ``.parquet`` or ``.csv``. It is written
        at exactly this path, and its directory must already exist.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        ``records``, unchanged.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import tempfile, pathlib
    >>> import scopusflow as sf
    >>> path = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "baseline.csv"
    >>> _ = sf.write_records(sf.example_records(), path)
    >>> len(sf.read_records(path))
    138
    """
    if not isinstance(records, pd.DataFrame):
        raise ValueError("records must be a record frame.")
    fmt = _format(path)
    if fmt == "csv":
        records.to_csv(path, index=False, lineterminator="\n")
        return records
    pa, pq = _pyarrow()
    safe = json_safe(records.attrs)
    block = json.dumps({"schema": _SCHEMA, "attrs": safe}, allow_nan=False)
    # Recent pyarrow copies attrs into its own pandas metadata, and warns and
    # drops them when they are not JSON. A shallow copy carrying the safe form
    # gives it something it can write and leaves the caller's frame alone.
    shallow = records.copy(deep=False)
    shallow.attrs = safe
    table = pa.Table.from_pandas(shallow, preserve_index=False)
    metadata = dict(table.schema.metadata or {})
    metadata[_METADATA_KEY] = block.encode("utf-8")
    pq.write_table(table.replace_schema_metadata(metadata), path)
    return records

Read a record set saved by :func:write_records.

Both formats come back with the record schema imposed: the text columns, scopus_id among them, as strings, and year and citations as nullable integers. A CSV left to pandas' own inference reads an all-digit identifier as a number, or as a float once one identifier is missing, and a de-duplicating :func:scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine then matches none of its records against a fresh harvest. The columns fields="extended" adds are read the same way, open_access as a nullable integer and the rest as strings, so an ISSN such as "00368075" keeps its leading zeros.

A parquet file comes back with the provenance it was saved with in attrs, so its search record reads as the original's did. A parquet file written by DataFrame.to_parquet under pandas 2.1 or later returns the attrs pandas stored. A CSV file carries none.

def read_records(path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a record set saved by :func:`write_records`.

    Both formats come back with the record schema imposed: the text columns,
    ``scopus_id`` among them, as strings, and ``year`` and ``citations`` as
    nullable integers. A CSV left to pandas' own inference reads an all-digit
    identifier as a number, or as a float once one identifier is missing, and
    a de-duplicating :func:`scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine` then matches
    none of its records against a fresh harvest. The columns
    ``fields="extended"`` adds are read the same way, ``open_access`` as a
    nullable integer and the rest as strings, so an ISSN such as
    ``"00368075"`` keeps its leading zeros.

    A parquet file comes back with the provenance it was saved with in
    ``attrs``, so its search record reads as the original's did. A parquet
    file written by ``DataFrame.to_parquet`` under pandas 2.1 or later
    returns the ``attrs`` pandas stored. A CSV file carries none.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path:
        The file to read, ending in ``.parquet`` or ``.csv``.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        The records, with any provenance in ``attrs``.
    """
    fmt = _format(path)
    if fmt == "parquet":
        _, pq = _pyarrow()
    if not Path(path).exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"File not found: {path}")
    if fmt == "csv":
        frame = _read_csv_records(path)
        attrs: dict = {}
    else:
        table = pq.read_table(path)
        frame = table.to_pandas()
        attrs = _stored_attrs(table.schema.metadata, frame.attrs, path)
        for column in _CHECKPOINT_TEXT:
            if column in frame.columns:
                frame[column] = frame[column].astype("string")
        frame = _as_whole_numbers(frame)
    frame.attrs = attrs
    return frame

to_bibtex(records)

Render records as a BibTeX string, one entry per row, with citation keys made unique within the export.

A set retrieved with fields="extended" (see :func:scopusflow.records.to_records) carries each record's Scopus document type, and the entry is typed by it. A conference paper (cp) or conference review (cr) becomes an @inproceedings, a book chapter (ch) an @incollection and a book (bk) a @book. Every other record, and every record of a set retrieved with the core fields, is an @article. The source title of a conference paper or chapter goes under booktitle, braced as the title is, and a journal article's under journal. A book in a book series gives the series under series, and a book outside a series, whose source title Scopus gives as the book's own, names no source. The entries also carry volume, number, pages (101--117), issn and, under view="COMPLETE", abstract and keywords, joined by commas. A value the record lacks is left out, never filled in.

Names are written family name first, with a comma. A STANDARD-view name such as Zhang F., which BibTeX would read as given name Zhang and family name F., is written Zhang, F., and run-together initials are spaced (Kitchin, J. R.), since BibTeX takes J.R. for one given name. Names that already carry a comma, as under COMPLETE, and names given first are written as they stand. The authors column and the citation keys are unchanged. In the title, every word with a capital after its first letter is braced ({DNA}, {CRISPR-Cas9}), so bibliography styles cannot lower-case it.

def to_bibtex(records: pd.DataFrame) -> str:
    """Render records as a BibTeX string, one entry per row, with citation keys
    made unique within the export.

    A set retrieved with ``fields="extended"`` (see
    :func:`scopusflow.records.to_records`) carries each record's Scopus
    document type, and the entry is typed by it. A conference paper (``cp``)
    or conference review (``cr``) becomes an ``@inproceedings``, a book chapter
    (``ch``) an ``@incollection`` and a book (``bk``) a ``@book``. Every other
    record, and every record of a set retrieved with the core fields, is an
    ``@article``. The source title of a conference paper or chapter goes under
    ``booktitle``, braced as the title is, and a journal article's under
    ``journal``. A book in a book series gives the series under ``series``, and
    a book outside a series, whose source title Scopus gives as the book's own,
    names no source. The entries also carry ``volume``, ``number``, ``pages``
    (``101--117``), ``issn`` and, under ``view="COMPLETE"``, ``abstract`` and
    ``keywords``, joined by commas. A value the record lacks is left out, never
    filled in.

    Names are written family name first, with a comma. A STANDARD-view name
    such as ``Zhang F.``, which BibTeX would read as given name ``Zhang`` and
    family name ``F.``, is written ``Zhang, F.``, and run-together initials are
    spaced (``Kitchin, J. R.``), since BibTeX takes ``J.R.`` for one given name.
    Names that already carry a comma, as under COMPLETE, and names given first
    are written as they stand. The ``authors`` column and the citation keys are
    unchanged. In the title, every word with a capital after its first letter
    is braced (``{DNA}``, ``{CRISPR-Cas9}``), so bibliography styles cannot
    lower-case it."""
    if not isinstance(records, pd.DataFrame):
        raise ValueError("records must be a pandas DataFrame.")
    rows = [row for _, row in records.iterrows()]
    keys = _disambiguate(
        [_bibtex_key(r.get("authors"), r.get("year"), r.get("scopus_id")) for r in rows]
    )
    return "\n\n".join(_bibtex_entry(r, k) for r, k in zip(rows, keys, strict=True))

Keywords are split at the " | " the Search API joins them with and at the "; " :func:scopusflow.abstract.scopus_abstract joins its own with. A value the record lacks is left out, never filled in.

The file is UTF-8, with no escaping beyond what JSON requires, sorted keys, no spaces between tokens and one line feed at the end, so the same corpus gives the same bytes from either twin. allow_nan=False stops the write before any file is opened should a NaN reach the document, since JSON has no such value. path is written exactly as given, and its parent directory is assumed to exist already.

def write_corpus(corpus: pd.DataFrame, path, id: str) -> dict:
    """Write the corpus to ``path`` as JSON in theoryforge's corpus schema.

    The document is :func:`to_theoryforge_corpus`'s, which describes the keys,
    the keywords and the ``provenance`` block, and it is returned too. The
    file is UTF-8, with no escaping beyond what JSON requires, sorted keys, no
    spaces between tokens and one line feed at the end, so the same corpus
    gives the same bytes from either twin. ``allow_nan=False`` stops the write
    before any file is opened should a ``NaN`` reach the document, since JSON
    has no such value. ``path`` is written exactly as given, and its parent
    directory is assumed to exist already.
    """
    doc = to_theoryforge_corpus(corpus, id)
    text = json.dumps(doc, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                      ensure_ascii=False, allow_nan=False)
    Path(path).write_bytes((text + "\n").encode("utf-8"))
    return doc

to_theoryforge_corpus(corpus, id)

The corpus as a document in theoryforge's corpus schema, as a dict.

Turns a :func:corpus result into the literature corpus that theoryforge's read_corpus, litmap and landscape read, following the corpus schema theoryforge publishes (schema/corpus.schema.json in its repository). :func:write_corpus writes the same document to a JSON file. Neither imports theoryforge, and neither makes a request.

theoryforge compares references as exact strings, so each cited work gets one key across the whole corpus, its Scopus identifier, as scopus:<id>. Scopus gives a cited work's DOI in some bibliographies only, and in different cases. A key built from the DOI wherever there is one would therefore split one work into several nodes and lose the co-citation edges between them. A reference that carries only a DOI takes the Scopus identifier that a document or reference elsewhere in the corpus pairs with the same DOI, the documents' own identifiers counting first. A DOI that nothing pairs with is keyed as doi:<doi>, without its resolver prefix and with its ASCII letters lower-cased, since DOIs are case-insensitive over ASCII (DOI Handbook, section 2.4). A reference with neither is dropped, and a UserWarning says how many. Each document is keyed the same way, from its scopus_id or else from an id that is a DOI or a Scopus identifier, so a citation of a document in the corpus and the document itself share one key. A document with neither raises ValueError.

Keywords are trimmed, lower-cased with str.lower() and made unique, keeping the first of each, and empty ones are dropped, so "Graphene" and "graphene " count as one keyword. The R twin lower-cases with tolower(). The two agree on the Latin, Greek and Cyrillic letters in common use and differ on a few special cases, such as the Turkish capital I with a dot and a capital sigma ending a word, which Python writes as a final sigma. A missing year is written as null, whether it is None, NaN or pd.NA, and a whole-number year of any dtype as a plain integer. A missing title is left out, since the schema admits a null year and not a null title.

The document also carries a provenance object, which the schema admits beside its own fields: source ("Scopus via scopusflow <version>"), query, retrieved_at (in UTC, as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ), keywords, n_records, n_references_dropped and n_records_without_keywords. query, retrieved_at and keywords come from the attrs that :func:corpus attaches, and are None (null) when the frame lacks them. query is a string, or a list of strings when the records were searched with several expressions. Author keywords can come back empty under some entitlements (see :func:scopus_abstract), which leaves theoryforge's keyword themes empty whatever the writer does, and n_records_without_keywords shows when that happened.

id is a non-empty string naming the corpus, written as its top-level id. It is required, since a :func:corpus result carries no name of its own. Returns a dict with id, provenance, records and schema_version ("1.0").

def to_theoryforge_corpus(corpus: pd.DataFrame, id: str) -> dict:
    """The corpus as a document in theoryforge's corpus schema, as a dict.

    Turns a :func:`corpus` result into the literature corpus that
    theoryforge's ``read_corpus``, ``litmap`` and ``landscape`` read, following
    the corpus schema theoryforge publishes (``schema/corpus.schema.json`` in
    its repository). :func:`write_corpus` writes the same document to a JSON
    file. Neither imports theoryforge, and neither makes a request.

    theoryforge compares references as exact strings, so each cited work gets
    one key across the whole corpus, its Scopus identifier, as
    ``scopus:<id>``. Scopus gives a cited work's DOI in some bibliographies
    only, and in different cases. A key built from the DOI wherever there is
    one would therefore split one work into several nodes and lose
    the co-citation edges between them. A reference that carries only a DOI
    takes the Scopus identifier that a document or reference
    elsewhere in the corpus pairs with the same DOI, the documents' own
    identifiers counting first. A DOI that nothing pairs with is keyed as
    ``doi:<doi>``, without its resolver prefix and with its ASCII letters
    lower-cased, since DOIs are case-insensitive over ASCII (DOI Handbook,
    section 2.4). A reference with neither is dropped, and a ``UserWarning``
    says how many. Each document is keyed the same way, from its
    ``scopus_id`` or else from an ``id`` that is a DOI or a Scopus
    identifier, so a citation of a document in the corpus and the document
    itself share one key. A document with neither raises ``ValueError``.

    Keywords are trimmed, lower-cased with ``str.lower()`` and made unique,
    keeping the first of each, and empty ones are dropped, so ``"Graphene"``
    and ``"graphene "`` count as one keyword. The R twin lower-cases with
    ``tolower()``. The two agree on the Latin, Greek and Cyrillic letters in
    common use and differ on a few special cases, such as the Turkish capital
    I with a dot and a capital sigma ending a word, which Python writes as a
    final sigma. A missing year is written as ``null``,
    whether it is ``None``, ``NaN`` or ``pd.NA``, and a whole-number year of
    any dtype as a plain integer. A missing title is left out, since the
    schema admits a null year and not a null title.

    The document also carries a ``provenance`` object, which the schema
    admits beside its own fields: ``source`` (``"Scopus via scopusflow
    <version>"``), ``query``, ``retrieved_at`` (in UTC, as
    ``YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ``), ``keywords``, ``n_records``,
    ``n_references_dropped`` and ``n_records_without_keywords``. ``query``,
    ``retrieved_at`` and ``keywords`` come from the ``attrs`` that
    :func:`corpus` attaches, and are ``None`` (``null``) when the frame lacks
    them. ``query`` is a string, or a list of strings when the records were
    searched with several expressions. Author keywords can come back empty
    under some entitlements (see :func:`scopus_abstract`), which leaves
    theoryforge's keyword themes empty whatever the writer does, and
    ``n_records_without_keywords`` shows when that happened.

    ``id`` is a non-empty string naming the corpus, written as its top-level
    ``id``. It is required, since a :func:`corpus` result carries no name of
    its own. Returns a dict with ``id``, ``provenance``, ``records`` and
    ``schema_version`` (``"1.0"``).
    """
    if not isinstance(id, str) or not id.strip():
        raise ValueError(
            "id must be a non-empty string naming the corpus, since a corpus() "
            "result carries no name of its own."
        )
    if not isinstance(corpus, pd.DataFrame) or not set(_CORPUS_COLUMNS) <= set(corpus.columns):
        raise ValueError(
            f"corpus must be a DataFrame with {list(_CORPUS_COLUMNS)} columns "
            "(as corpus() returns)."
        )
    n = len(corpus)

    # Each document's own identifiers: its scopus_id, else an id that is a
    # Scopus identifier (a corpus looked up by scopus_id), and an id that is
    # a DOI (a corpus looked up by DOI).
    ids = [_text(v) for v in corpus["id"]]
    record_doi = [d if d is not None and _DOI_SHAPE.match(d) else None
                  for d in map(_doi, ids)]
    given = corpus["scopus_id"] if "scopus_id" in corpus.columns else [None] * n
    record_sid = [
        _sid(s) or (_sid(i) if d is None else None)
        for s, i, d in zip(given, ids, record_doi, strict=True)
    ]
    cited = [_cited(refs) for refs in corpus["references"]]

    # Every document and reference carrying both says which identifier a DOI
    # belongs to. The first pair met wins, the documents' own coming first.
    sid_of_doi: dict[str, str] = {}
    pairs = list(zip(record_sid, record_doi, strict=True))
    pairs += [pair for refs in cited for pair in refs]
    for sid, doi in pairs:
        if sid is not None and doi is not None:
            sid_of_doi.setdefault(doi, sid)

    def key(sid, doi):
        sid = sid or sid_of_doi.get(doi)
        if sid is not None:
            return f"scopus:{sid}"
        return f"doi:{doi}" if doi is not None else None

    record_key = [key(s, d) for s, d in zip(record_sid, record_doi, strict=True)]
    unkeyed = [i for i, k in enumerate(record_key) if k is None]
    if unkeyed:
        shown = ", ".join(str(i) for i in unkeyed[:10])
        raise ValueError(
            f"{len(unkeyed)} record(s) of corpus (row {shown}, counting from 0) "
            "carry neither a Scopus identifier nor a DOI to key on."
        )

    dropped = 0
    records = []
    for row, own_key, refs in zip(corpus.itertuples(index=False), record_key, cited,
                                  strict=True):
        keys = [key(s, d) for s, d in refs]
        dropped += sum(k is None for k in keys)
        record = {
            "id": own_key,
            "keywords": _keywords(row.keywords),
            "references": list(dict.fromkeys(k for k in keys if k is not None)),
        }
        if isinstance(row.title, str) and row.title.strip():
            record["title"] = row.title.strip()
        record["year"] = _year(row.year)
        records.append(record)
    if dropped:
        warnings.warn(
            f"Dropped {dropped} reference(s) with neither a Scopus identifier nor "
            "a DOI, which no key can name.",
            UserWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    # Imported here: __version__ is bound only once the package's own imports,
    # this module's among them, have returned.
    from . import __version__

    kind = corpus.attrs.get("keywords")
    provenance = {
        "keywords": kind if isinstance(kind, str) else None,
        "n_records": n,
        "n_records_without_keywords": sum(not r["keywords"] for r in records),
        "n_references_dropped": dropped,
        "query": _query(corpus.attrs.get("query")),
        "retrieved_at": _utc(corpus.attrs.get("retrieved_at")),
        "source": f"Scopus via scopusflow {__version__}",
    }
    return {"id": id, "provenance": provenance, "records": records, "schema_version": "1.0"}
