scopus_search_report(x, plan=None, file=None)

Assemble a reproducible record of a Scopus search.

Turns a harvest, or a plan not yet run, into the search-strategy record a systematic review has to report: what was searched, exactly how, when, how much came back, and how much the API said there was. The record prints as a readable report, formats as a methods paragraph fit to paste into a manuscript, and writes as Markdown. The reporting standard it follows is PRISMA-S (Rethlefsen et al., 2021), together with the identification counts of the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.

Everything in the record comes from the objects handed to it. The dates of the search are the retrieved_at and retrieved_until attributes :func:scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan attaches, never the current time. A harvest resumed over several days, or a baseline merged with its update, is dated from its first retrieval to its last. PRISMA-S item 13 then gives the date of the last search, as the checklist asks. Stamps that fall on one UTC day give that single date. The years are those the cells' limits sent, and years with gaps between them are listed, since a span would claim years no cell searched. The number of records the API reported as matching is the per-cell accounting in cell_totals, or, for a set from a single search, its total_results, never an inference from the number of rows; and the duplicates removed are those :func:scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine recorded removing, matched by the rule it recorded. Where an attribute is absent, as it is for a frame read back from CSV, for the bundled corpus, and for a harvest with a cell resumed from a checkpoint written without a manifest by an earlier version of scopusflow, the record says the field is unrecorded and fills nothing in. This matters most for completeness: a harvest whose reported total is unknown is never described as exhaustive.

A harvest stopped through should_stop, as the app's Cancel stops one, says so. The record gives how many of the planned cells ran and which years they covered, marks the rest "not run" and calls the harvest incomplete, keeping the totals the cells that ran recorded. The R twin's scopus_fetch_plan() can also cap the records per cell, and its record then names the cap in the cells it stopped, the completeness line and item 9. A frame carrying attrs["max_results"] is described the same way here, so the two records stay one rendering, although :func:~scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan takes no cap and so never records one.

The PRISMA-S map is decided the same way. Items the package holds evidence for (the database and platform, that Scopus was searched on its own, the full strategy and the limits where a plan records them, the date, the totals, and de-duplication where it was performed) are listed as supplied. Without a plan, the year limit is unrecorded, not absent, and the record says so. The rest, among them peer review of the strategy, grey literature and citation searching, are listed as the author's to supply, because the package has no way to know them.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x

A records frame, which supplies the counts and the retrieval provenance and, through attrs["plan"], the plan; or a bare :class:~scopusflow.plan.SearchPlan for a search not yet run. The attributes are read in the JSON-safe forms :func:~scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan writes (the plan as a dict, the time as ISO 8601 text, the cell totals as a list of dicts) and in the richer forms a guide may set by hand (a SearchPlan, a datetime, a DataFrame).

required plan SearchPlan | None

The plan describing x. Supply it when a records frame does not carry one, for instance one read back from CSV or a merged set. An explicit plan takes precedence over the one x carries. A one-cell plan supplied for a frame without per-cell counts takes the frame's own row count and total_results.

None file

Path at which to write the record as Markdown. A file is written only when this is supplied, and only to the exact path given, so nothing is written to the working directory unless asked.

None

Returns:

Type Description SearchReport

The record. print shows it, report.format(style="paragraph") gives the methods paragraph.

References

Rethlefsen, M. L., Kirtley, S., Waffenschmidt, S., Ayala, A. P., Moher, D., Page, M. J., & Koffel, J. B. (2021). PRISMA-S: an extension to the PRISMA Statement for Reporting Literature Searches in Systematic Reviews. Systematic Reviews, 10, 39. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-020-01542-z

Examples:

A search described but not yet run. The record says so throughout rather than implying figures it cannot have.

>>> import scopusflow as sf
>>> plan = sf.SearchPlan('"graphene supercapacitor"', years=range(2015, 2025),
...                      field="TITLE-ABS-KEY", partition="year")
>>> report = sf.scopus_search_report(plan)
>>> report.n_records is None
True

The same search after a harvest. The bundled corpus stands in for one, since Scopus records may not be redistributed, so the attributes a live retrieval records are set here by hand. Their values are illustrative, and the records came from OpenAlex, so the record below describes no search that was run.

>>> from datetime import datetime, timezone
>>> records = sf.example_records()
>>> records.attrs["plan"] = plan
>>> records.attrs["retrieved_at"] = datetime(2026, 7, 22, 9, 15,
...                                          tzinfo=timezone.utc)
>>> records.attrs["scopusflow_version"] = "0.3.0"
>>> report = sf.scopus_search_report(records)
>>> report.n_records
138
>>> "22 July 2026" in report.format(style="paragraph")
True

def scopus_search_report(x, plan: SearchPlan | None = None, file=None) -> SearchReport:
    """Assemble a reproducible record of a Scopus search.

    Turns a harvest, or a plan not yet run, into the search-strategy record a
    systematic review has to report: what was searched, exactly how, when, how
    much came back, and how much the API said there was. The record prints as a
    readable report, formats as a methods paragraph fit to paste into a
    manuscript, and writes as Markdown. The reporting standard it follows is
    PRISMA-S (Rethlefsen et al., 2021), together with the identification counts
    of the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.

    Everything in the record comes from the objects handed to it. The dates of
    the search are the ``retrieved_at`` and ``retrieved_until`` attributes
    :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan` attaches, never the current time. A
    harvest resumed over several days, or a baseline merged with its update,
    is dated from its first retrieval to its last. PRISMA-S item 13 then gives
    the date of the last search, as the checklist asks. Stamps that fall on
    one UTC day give that single date. The years are those the cells'
    limits sent, and years with gaps between them are listed, since a span
    would claim years no cell searched. The number of records the API reported
    as matching is the per-cell accounting in ``cell_totals``, or, for a set
    from a single search, its ``total_results``, never an inference from the
    number of rows; and the duplicates removed are those
    :func:`scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine` recorded removing, matched by the
    rule it recorded. Where an
    attribute is absent, as it is for a frame read back from CSV, for the
    bundled corpus, and for a harvest with a cell resumed from a checkpoint
    written without a manifest by an earlier version of scopusflow, the record
    says the field is unrecorded and fills nothing in. This matters
    most for completeness: a harvest whose reported total is unknown is never
    described as exhaustive.

    A harvest stopped through ``should_stop``, as the app's Cancel stops one,
    says so. The record gives how many of the planned cells ran and which
    years they covered, marks the rest "not run" and calls the harvest
    incomplete, keeping the totals the cells that ran recorded. The R twin's
    ``scopus_fetch_plan()`` can also cap the records per cell, and its record
    then names the cap in the cells it stopped, the completeness line and
    item 9. A frame carrying ``attrs["max_results"]`` is described the same
    way here, so the two records stay one rendering, although
    :func:`~scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan` takes no cap and so never records one.

    The PRISMA-S map is decided the same way. Items the package holds evidence
    for (the database and platform, that Scopus was searched on its own, the
    full strategy and the limits where a plan records them, the date, the
    totals, and de-duplication where it was performed) are listed as supplied.
    Without a plan, the year limit is unrecorded, not absent, and the record
    says so. The rest, among them peer review of the strategy, grey literature
    and citation searching, are listed as the author's to supply, because the
    package has no way to know them.

    Parameters
    ----------
    x:
        A records frame, which supplies the counts and the retrieval provenance
        and, through ``attrs["plan"]``, the plan; or a bare
        :class:`~scopusflow.plan.SearchPlan` for a search not yet run. The
        attributes are read in the JSON-safe forms
        :func:`~scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan` writes (the plan as a dict, the
        time as ISO 8601 text, the cell totals as a list of dicts) and in the
        richer forms a guide may set by hand (a ``SearchPlan``, a
        ``datetime``, a DataFrame).
    plan:
        The plan describing ``x``. Supply it when a records frame does not carry
        one, for instance one read back from CSV or a merged set. An explicit
        plan takes precedence over the one ``x`` carries. A one-cell plan
        supplied for a frame without per-cell counts takes the frame's own row
        count and ``total_results``.
    file:
        Path at which to write the record as Markdown. A file is written only
        when this is supplied, and only to the exact path given, so nothing is
        written to the working directory unless asked.

    Returns
    -------
    SearchReport
        The record. ``print`` shows it, ``report.format(style="paragraph")``
        gives the methods paragraph.

    References
    ----------
    Rethlefsen, M. L., Kirtley, S., Waffenschmidt, S., Ayala, A. P., Moher, D.,
    Page, M. J., & Koffel, J. B. (2021). PRISMA-S: an extension to the PRISMA
    Statement for Reporting Literature Searches in Systematic Reviews.
    *Systematic Reviews*, *10*, 39. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-020-01542-z

    Examples
    --------
    A search described but not yet run. The record says so throughout rather
    than implying figures it cannot have.

    >>> import scopusflow as sf
    >>> plan = sf.SearchPlan('"graphene supercapacitor"', years=range(2015, 2025),
    ...                      field="TITLE-ABS-KEY", partition="year")
    >>> report = sf.scopus_search_report(plan)
    >>> report.n_records is None
    True

    The same search after a harvest. The bundled corpus stands in for one, since
    Scopus records may not be redistributed, so the attributes a live retrieval
    records are set here by hand. Their values are illustrative, and the records
    came from OpenAlex, so the record below describes no search that was run.

    >>> from datetime import datetime, timezone
    >>> records = sf.example_records()
    >>> records.attrs["plan"] = plan
    >>> records.attrs["retrieved_at"] = datetime(2026, 7, 22, 9, 15,
    ...                                          tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    >>> records.attrs["scopusflow_version"] = "0.3.0"
    >>> report = sf.scopus_search_report(records)
    >>> report.n_records
    138
    >>> "22 July 2026" in report.format(style="paragraph")
    True
    """
    if plan is not None and not isinstance(plan, SearchPlan):
        raise ValueError("The plan must be a search plan.")
    if isinstance(x, SearchPlan):
        records = None
        plan = plan or x
    elif isinstance(x, pd.DataFrame):
        records = x
        if plan is None:
            plan = as_plan(x.attrs.get("plan"))
    else:
        raise ValueError("A search report needs a record set or a search plan.")

    report = _build(records, plan)

    if file is not None:
        if not isinstance(file, (str, bytes)) and not hasattr(file, "__fspath__"):
            raise ValueError("The file must be a single non-empty path.")
        if isinstance(file, (str, bytes)) and not str(file).strip():
            raise ValueError("The file must be a single non-empty path.")
        # Newline fixed to LF, so the record is byte-identical on every platform
        # and against the R twin, which writes its text artefacts the same way.
        with open(file, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as fh:
            fh.write(_render_markdown(report) + "\n")
    return report

The fields a search record is built from, and its three renderings.

Every attribute is either what the objects recorded or None, which the renderings spell out as unrecorded. cells is a frame of cell, limit, n_records and reported_total; prisma a frame of item, name, source ("record" or "author") and note. searched_at and searched_until are the earliest and latest retrieval times. max_results is the cap on records per cell a set records. stopped_early, cells_planned and cells_run describe a harvest stopped before its last cell, not_run lists the cells it never reached and years_run the years of those it ran. dedupe_rule and doi_conflicts are the rule :func:scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine matched records by and the DOIs it left shared across identifiers.

@dataclass(eq=False)
class SearchReport:
    """The fields a search record is built from, and its three renderings.

    Every attribute is either what the objects recorded or ``None``, which the
    renderings spell out as unrecorded. ``cells`` is a frame of ``cell``,
    ``limit``, ``n_records`` and ``reported_total``; ``prisma`` a frame of
    ``item``, ``name``, ``source`` (``"record"`` or ``"author"``) and ``note``.
    ``searched_at`` and ``searched_until`` are the earliest and latest
    retrieval times. ``max_results`` is the cap on records per cell a set
    records. ``stopped_early``, ``cells_planned`` and ``cells_run`` describe a
    harvest stopped before its last cell, ``not_run`` lists the cells it never
    reached and ``years_run`` the years of those it ran. ``dedupe_rule`` and
    ``doi_conflicts`` are the rule :func:`scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine`
    matched records by and the DOIs it left shared across identifiers.
    """

    database: str = "Scopus"
    platform: str = "Elsevier Scopus Search API"
    query: str | None = None
    field: str | None = None
    expression: list[str] | None = None
    view: str | None = None
    page_size: int | None = None
    paging: str | None = None
    max_results: int | None = None
    partition: str | None = None
    n_cells: int | None = None
    years: str | None = None
    years_run: str | None = None
    cells: pd.DataFrame = dataclass_field(default_factory=pd.DataFrame)
    searched_at: datetime | None = None
    searched_until: datetime | None = None
    version: str | None = None
    n_records: int | None = None
    n_with_doi: int | None = None
    reported_total: int | None = None
    cells_reported: int = 0
    stopped_early: bool = False
    cells_planned: int | None = None
    cells_run: int | None = None
    not_run: list[int] = dataclass_field(default_factory=list)
    records_combined: int | None = None
    duplicates_removed: int | None = None
    deduplicated: bool | None = None
    dedupe_rule: str | None = None
    doi_conflicts: int | None = None
    snippet: str | None = None
    prisma: pd.DataFrame = dataclass_field(default_factory=pd.DataFrame)

    def format(self, style: str = "report") -> str:
        """Render the record: ``"report"`` for the readable record ``print``
        shows, ``"paragraph"`` for the methods paragraph, or ``"markdown"`` for
        the whole record as Markdown, which is what ``file`` writes."""
        if style == "report":
            return _render_report(self)
        if style == "paragraph":
            return _render_paragraph(self)
        if style == "markdown":
            return _render_markdown(self)
        raise ValueError("style must be 'report', 'paragraph' or 'markdown'.")

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return _render_report(self)

    __repr__ = __str__

def format(self, style: str = "report") -> str:
    """Render the record: ``"report"`` for the readable record ``print``
    shows, ``"paragraph"`` for the methods paragraph, or ``"markdown"`` for
    the whole record as Markdown, which is what ``file`` writes."""
    if style == "report":

    if style == "paragraph":
        return _render_paragraph(self)
    if style == "markdown":
        return _render_markdown(self)
    raise ValueError("style must be 'report', 'paragraph' or 'markdown'.")

def extract_dois(records, dedupe: bool = True) -> list[str]:
    """Pull cleaned, optionally de-duplicated DOIs from records or a list."""
    dois = _clean(_as_dois(records))
    if not dedupe:
        return dois
    seen: set[str] = set()
    result: list[str] = []
    for d in dois:
        key = d.lower()
        if key not in seen:
            seen.add(key)
            result.append(d)
    return result

Compare the DOIs of two retrievals.

A record without a DOI cannot be compared this way, and Scopus gives no DOI to a share of what it indexes, more of it in the arts and humanities and among books and proceedings (Gorraiz et al., 2016). Such records are left out of the rows and counted in attrs. :func:diff_records compares the records themselves, matching on the Scopus identifier.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default old

Record frames or lists of DOIs, the earlier (old) and the later (new) retrieval.

required new

required

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

A doi column and a status column, where the status is added (in new only), removed (in old only) or unchanged (in both), compared without resolver prefixes and ignoring case. Rows are sorted by status then DOI, comparing code points, which the R twin's scopus_diff_dois() matches. The ints attrs["n_old_without_doi"] and attrs["n_new_without_doi"] count the records (or list entries) on each side that had no DOI and so were not compared.

References

Gorraiz, J., Melero-Fuentes, D., Gumpenberger, C., & Valderrama-Zurián, J.-C. (2016). Availability of digital object identifiers (DOIs) in Web of Science and Scopus. Journal of Informetrics, 10(1), 98–109. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2015.11.008

def diff_dois(old, new) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Compare the DOIs of two retrievals.

    A record without a DOI cannot be compared this way, and Scopus gives no
    DOI to a share of what it indexes, more of it in the arts and humanities
    and among books and proceedings (Gorraiz et al., 2016). Such records are
    left out of the rows and counted in ``attrs``.
    :func:`diff_records` compares the records themselves, matching on the
    Scopus identifier.

    Parameters
    ----------
    old, new:
        Record frames or lists of DOIs, the earlier (``old``) and the later
        (``new``) retrieval.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        A ``doi`` column and a ``status`` column, where the status is
        ``added`` (in ``new`` only), ``removed`` (in ``old`` only) or
        ``unchanged`` (in both), compared without resolver prefixes and
        ignoring case. Rows are sorted by status then DOI, comparing code
        points, which the R twin's ``scopus_diff_dois()`` matches. The ints
        ``attrs["n_old_without_doi"]`` and ``attrs["n_new_without_doi"]``
        count the records (or list entries) on each side that had no DOI and
        so were not compared.

    References
    ----------
    Gorraiz, J., Melero-Fuentes, D., Gumpenberger, C., & Valderrama-Zurián,
    J.-C. (2016). Availability of digital object identifiers (DOIs) in Web of
    Science and Scopus. *Journal of Informetrics*, *10*(1), 98–109.
    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2015.11.008
    """
    old_raw, new_raw = _as_dois(old), _as_dois(new)
    old_d, new_d = extract_dois(old_raw), extract_dois(new_raw)
    old_keys = {d.lower() for d in old_d}
    new_keys = {d.lower() for d in new_d}
    rows = (
        [(d, "added") for d in new_d if d.lower() not in old_keys]
        + [(d, "removed") for d in old_d if d.lower() not in new_keys]
        + [(d, "unchanged") for d in new_d if d.lower() in old_keys]
    )
    # Sorted here, comparing code points, so that the order cannot depend on
    # how a pandas version or its Arrow backend sorts text.
    rows.sort(key=lambda row: (_DOI_STATUSES.index(row[1]), row[0]))
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["doi", "status"])
    df.attrs["n_old_without_doi"] = sum(_clean_one(d) is None for d in old_raw)
    df.attrs["n_new_without_doi"] = sum(_clean_one(d) is None for d in new_raw)
    return df

diff_records(old, new)

Compare two retrievals record by record.

Identifies which records were added, removed or unchanged between an earlier and a later retrieval, and gives each record's citation count in both. :func:diff_dois compares DOIs alone, and this function compares the records themselves, matched as scopus_combine(dedupe=True) matches them. A record without a DOI is therefore still tracked by its Scopus identifier, and two records under one DOI are not taken for one.

Two records are one record when they share a Scopus identifier, or when they share a DOI and one of them lacks an identifier. DOIs are compared as :func:extract_dois compares them, without resolver prefixes and ignoring case. Records with different identifiers are never matched, even under one DOI, since Scopus gives one DOI to distinct papers as well as holding duplicate records of one paper (:func:scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine gives the sources).

A record found in one retrieval only is a conflict where the other retrieval gives its DOI to a different record. It may have been re-indexed under a new identifier, or it may be a distinct paper sharing the DOI. Only the two records themselves can tell, so it is counted neither as added nor as removed. A record without an identifier whose DOI two identified records carry is in the same position. A record with neither an identifier nor a DOI cannot be matched at all, and is left out of the rows and counted.

scopus_id is the identifier the record was matched on, missing for a record matched on its DOI alone. doi is the DOI without its resolver prefix, in the case the record gives it. doi, title and year come from the later retrieval where it holds the record and gives a value, and from the earlier one otherwise, while citations_old and citations_new come from each retrieval in turn. Where one retrieval holds a record more than once, the first value it gives is used.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default old

Record frames with a scopus_id or a doi column, the earlier (old) and the later (new) retrieval. The title, year and citations columns are read where present.

required new

Record frames with a scopus_id or a doi column, the earlier (old) and the later (new) retrieval. The title, year and citations columns are read where present.

required

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

One row per record, with the columns status, scopus_id, doi, title, year, citations_old and citations_new. The status is added (in new only), removed (in old only), conflict or unchanged (in both). Rows are sorted in that order of status, then by DOI, identifier and title, comparing code points, which the R twin's scopus_diff_records() matches. The ints attrs["n_old_without_id_or_doi"] and attrs["n_new_without_id_or_doi"] count the records on each side that carried neither key and so were not compared.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

When old or new is not a frame, or has neither a scopus_id nor a doi column.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import scopusflow as sf
>>> old = pd.DataFrame({"scopus_id": ["85000000001", "85000000002"],
...                     "doi": ["10.5555/a", "10.5555/c"]})
>>> new = pd.DataFrame({"scopus_id": ["85000000001", "85000000033"],
...                     "doi": ["10.5555/a", "10.5555/c"]})
>>> list(sf.diff_records(old, new)["status"])
['conflict', 'conflict', 'unchanged']

def diff_records(old, new) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Compare two retrievals record by record.

    Identifies which records were added, removed or unchanged between an
    earlier and a later retrieval, and gives each record's citation count in
    both. :func:`diff_dois` compares DOIs alone, and this function compares
    the records themselves, matched as ``scopus_combine(dedupe=True)`` matches
    them. A record without a DOI is therefore still tracked by its Scopus
    identifier, and two records under one DOI are not taken for one.

    Two records are one record when they share a Scopus identifier, or when
    they share a DOI and one of them lacks an identifier. DOIs are compared as
    :func:`extract_dois` compares them, without resolver prefixes and ignoring
    case. Records with different identifiers are never matched, even under one
    DOI, since Scopus gives one DOI to distinct papers as well as holding
    duplicate records of one paper
    (:func:`scopusflow.combine.scopus_combine` gives the sources).

    A record found in one retrieval only is a ``conflict`` where the other
    retrieval gives its DOI to a different record. It may have been re-indexed
    under a new identifier, or it may be a distinct paper sharing the DOI.
    Only the two records themselves can tell, so it is counted neither as
    added nor as removed. A record without an identifier whose DOI two
    identified records carry is in the same position. A record with neither an
    identifier nor a DOI cannot be matched at all, and is left out of the rows
    and counted.

    ``scopus_id`` is the identifier the record was matched on, missing for a
    record matched on its DOI alone. ``doi`` is the DOI without its resolver
    prefix, in the case the record gives it. ``doi``, ``title`` and ``year``
    come from the later retrieval where it holds the record and gives a value,
    and from the earlier one otherwise, while ``citations_old`` and
    ``citations_new`` come from each retrieval in turn. Where one retrieval
    holds a record more than once, the first value it gives is used.

    Parameters
    ----------
    old, new:
        Record frames with a ``scopus_id`` or a ``doi`` column, the earlier
        (``old``) and the later (``new``) retrieval. The ``title``, ``year``
        and ``citations`` columns are read where present.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        One row per record, with the columns ``status``, ``scopus_id``,
        ``doi``, ``title``, ``year``, ``citations_old`` and
        ``citations_new``. The status is ``added`` (in ``new`` only),
        ``removed`` (in ``old`` only), ``conflict`` or ``unchanged`` (in
        both). Rows are sorted in that order of status, then by DOI,
        identifier and title, comparing code points, which the R twin's
        ``scopus_diff_records()`` matches. The ints
        ``attrs["n_old_without_id_or_doi"]`` and
        ``attrs["n_new_without_id_or_doi"]`` count the records on each side
        that carried neither key and so were not compared.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        When ``old`` or ``new`` is not a frame, or has neither a ``scopus_id``
        nor a ``doi`` column.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> import scopusflow as sf
    >>> old = pd.DataFrame({"scopus_id": ["85000000001", "85000000002"],
    ...                     "doi": ["10.5555/a", "10.5555/c"]})
    >>> new = pd.DataFrame({"scopus_id": ["85000000001", "85000000033"],
    ...                     "doi": ["10.5555/a", "10.5555/c"]})
    >>> list(sf.diff_records(old, new)["status"])
    ['conflict', 'conflict', 'unchanged']
    """
    # Imported here because combine imports this module for _clean_one.
    from .combine import _record_groups

    old_rows, new_rows = _diff_frame(old, "old"), _diff_frame(new, "new")
    rows = old_rows + new_rows
    later = [False] * len(old_rows) + [True] * len(new_rows)

    # The default de-duplication rule, applied across the two retrievals, so
    # the diff and a merge of the same two sets agree on which records are one.
    keys, _ = _record_groups(
        pd.DataFrame({"scopus_id": [r["scopus_id"] for r in rows],
                      "doi": [r["doi"] for r in rows]}, dtype=object),
        "id_or_shared_doi",
    )
    dois = [_clean_one(r["doi"]) for r in rows]
    doi_keys = [None if d is None else d.lower() for d in dois]
    keyed = [not key.startswith("row:") for key in keys]

    groups: dict[str, dict] = {}
    for i, key in enumerate(keys):
        if not keyed[i]:
            continue
        group = groups.setdefault(key, {"old": [], "new": []})
        group["new" if later[i] else "old"].append(i)

    old_dois = {k for k, side in zip(doi_keys, later, strict=True) if k and not side}
    new_dois = {k for k, side in zip(doi_keys, later, strict=True) if k and side}
    titles = [r["title"] for r in rows]
    years = [r["year"] for r in rows]
    citations = [r["citations"] for r in rows]

    def first(values, indices):
        """The first value the rows at ``indices`` give, or ``None``."""
        return next((values[i] for i in indices if _given(values[i])), None)

    def latest(values, group):
        """The later retrieval's value where it gives one, the earlier one's
        if not."""
        given = first(values, group["new"])
        return given if given is not None else first(values, group["old"])

    out = []
    for key, group in groups.items():
        if group["old"] and group["new"]:
            status = "unchanged"
        else:
            # A record in one retrieval only whose DOI the other retrieval
            # gives to a record of its own. That record is a different one, or
            # the two would share a key and the first would be in both.
            other = new_dois if group["old"] else old_dois
            indices = group["old"] or group["new"]
            clash = any(doi_keys[i] in other for i in indices if doi_keys[i])
            status = "conflict" if clash else ("removed" if group["old"] else "added")
        out.append({
            "status": status,
            # The identifier the record was matched on, which its key carries.
            "scopus_id": key[3:] if key.startswith("id:") else None,
            "doi": latest(dois, group),
            "title": latest(titles, group),
            "year": latest(years, group),
            "citations_old": first(citations, group["old"]),
            "citations_new": first(citations, group["new"]),
        })

    out.sort(key=lambda r: (_RECORD_STATUSES.index(r["status"]), _byte_order(r["doi"]),
                            _byte_order(r["scopus_id"]), _byte_order(r["title"])))
    frame = pd.DataFrame({
        "status": [r["status"] for r in out],
        "scopus_id": pd.array([r["scopus_id"] for r in out], dtype="string"),
        "doi": pd.array([r["doi"] for r in out], dtype="string"),
        "title": pd.array([r["title"] for r in out], dtype="string"),
        "year": pd.array([r["year"] for r in out], dtype="Int64"),
        "citations_old": pd.array([r["citations_old"] for r in out], dtype="Int64"),
        "citations_new": pd.array([r["citations_new"] for r in out], dtype="Int64"),
    }, columns=_RECORD_DIFF_COLUMNS)
    frame.attrs["n_old_without_id_or_doi"] = sum(
        not k and not side for k, side in zip(keyed, later, strict=True))
    frame.attrs["n_new_without_id_or_doi"] = sum(
        not k and side for k, side in zip(keyed, later, strict=True))
    return frame

scopus_trend(query, years, field=None, view='STANDARD', **kwargs)

Count Scopus hits for query in each of years without downloading them.

Each year is a cheap result-size lookup, so this gives a publication trend far faster than harvesting every record. field wraps the query in a Scopus field tag (see :data:scopusflow.query.FIELD_TAGS), the way :func:scopusflow.count.scopus_count and the R twin's scopus_trend() do; left None, the query is sent as given.

Each count is sent with refresh=True unless you pass refresh. pybliometrics keys its own response cache on the query string and view alone. Without refresh=True, it could answer a year with the number of rows an earlier harvest of the same query left there. refresh=False, or a number of days, opts in to that cache, and a year it answers is warned about. The key ignores keyword filters such as subj, so fold any filter into the query before you opt in.

The result records when the counts were taken, in attrs["retrieved_at"] as ISO 8601 text in UTC, as a harvest records its own. Scopus goes on indexing a year's publications after the year has begun, so a count for the year of retrieval is a count so far, and :func:scopusflow.plots.plot_trend says so from this time. A count answered from pybliometrics' cache is dated by its cache file, and the earliest time is kept. When a cached count's file time cannot be read, the attribute is left out, since a trend dated by its other counts would be dated later than that one.

Raises :class:scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowConfigError before any request when pybliometrics.init() has not been called in the session.

Source code in src/scopusflow/trend.py 
def scopus_trend(
    query: str,
    years: Sequence[int],
    field: str | None = None,
    view: str = "STANDARD",
    **kwargs,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Count Scopus hits for ``query`` in each of ``years`` without downloading them.

    Each year is a cheap result-size lookup, so this gives a publication trend
    far faster than harvesting every record. ``field`` wraps the query in a
    Scopus field tag (see :data:`scopusflow.query.FIELD_TAGS`), the way
    :func:`scopusflow.count.scopus_count` and the R twin's ``scopus_trend()``
    do; left ``None``, the query is sent as given.

    Each count is sent with ``refresh=True`` unless you pass ``refresh``.
    pybliometrics keys its own response cache on the query string and view
    alone. Without ``refresh=True``, it could answer a year with the number of
    rows an earlier harvest of the same query left there. ``refresh=False``,
    or a number of days, opts in to that cache, and a year it answers is
    warned about. The key ignores keyword filters such as ``subj``, so fold any
    filter into the query before you opt in.

    The result records when the counts were taken, in ``attrs["retrieved_at"]``
    as ISO 8601 text in UTC, as a harvest records its own. Scopus goes on
    indexing a year's publications after the year has begun, so a count for
    the year of retrieval is a count so far, and
    :func:`scopusflow.plots.plot_trend` says so from this time. A count answered
    from pybliometrics' cache is dated by its cache file, and the earliest time
    is kept. When a cached count's file time cannot be read, the attribute is
    left out, since a trend dated by its other counts would be dated later than
    that one.

    Raises :class:`scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowConfigError` before any
    request when ``pybliometrics.init()`` has not been called in the session.
    """
    if not query or not query.strip():
        raise ValueError("query must be a non-empty string.")
    # Checked offline first (see scopusflow.plan.SearchPlan), so a query the
    # API cannot run as written costs no request.
    _check_query(query, field)
    years = list(years)
    if not years:
        raise ValueError("years must be a non-empty sequence.")
    # Validated before it reaches the query: the year used to be
    # interpolated raw, so a float year sent the API "PUBYEAR IS 2015.0" while
    # the result was filed under 2015.
    years = _check_years(years)
    # Wrapped once, before the loop: the tag applies to the query alone, never
    # to the year
    # filter folded in beside it.
    query = wrap_field(query, field)
    kwargs.setdefault("refresh", True)
    require_init()

    from pybliometrics.scopus import ScopusSearch  # imported lazily; needs a key

    counts: dict[int, int] = {}
    cached: list = []
    for y in years:
        # Bracketed first when a top-level OR or AND NOT would otherwise take
        # the year filter from part of the query.
        year_query = _and_clause(query, f"PUBYEAR IS {y}")
        t0 = time.time()
        search = ScopusSearch(year_query, view=view, download=False, **kwargs)
        counts[y], written = result_size_and_time(
            search, t0, kwargs["refresh"], year_query, stacklevel=2
        )
        if written is not None:
            cached.append(written)
    out = _trend_frame(counts)
    # Dated as fetch_plan() dates its cells: a count the API gave by the time
    # the counting finished, a count from pybliometrics' cache by its file,
    # and the earliest kept, so the trend never claims fresher counts than
    # it holds.
    if UNDATED not in cached:
        out.attrs["retrieved_at"] = iso_utc(min([datetime.now(timezone.utc), *cached]))
    return out

year_counts(records, fill=True)

Count records per publication year, dropping rows with a missing year.

Returns a :data:TREND_COLUMNS frame sorted ascending by year, with both columns as plain integers.

With fill (the default), every year the records' searches covered is counted, a year without records as zero. :func:scopusflow.plots.plot_trend therefore draws the line down to zero there, where it used to run straight across the gap. The years searched are read from the plan in records.attrs["plan"], which :func:scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan attaches: the year of each cell under partition="year", and every year of the range under partition="none". A year no cell searched is not added, so a plan over 2015, 2016, 2019 and 2020 gives no row for 2017 or 2018. A harvest stopped before its last cell covers only the cells it ran. Without a plan, or with one that sent no year limit, the years run from the first year in the records to the last. A year that holds records keeps its row in every case, and a set in which no record has a year gives an empty frame. The R twin's autoplot() counts a record set's years by the same rule.

fill=False counts only the years that hold records, as earlier versions did.

The records' attrs["retrieved_at"] is carried to the result, so :func:scopusflow.plots.plot_trend can say when the last year plotted was still being indexed.

Source code in src/scopusflow/trend.py 
def year_counts(records: pd.DataFrame, fill: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Count records per publication year, dropping rows with a missing year.

    Returns a :data:`TREND_COLUMNS` frame sorted ascending by year, with both
    columns as plain integers.

    With ``fill`` (the default), every year the records' searches covered is
    counted, a year without records as zero. :func:`scopusflow.plots.plot_trend`
    therefore draws the line down to zero there, where it used to run straight
    across the gap. The years searched are read from the plan in
    ``records.attrs["plan"]``, which :func:`scopusflow.fetch.fetch_plan`
    attaches: the year of each cell under ``partition="year"``, and every year
    of the range under ``partition="none"``. A year no cell searched is not added, so a plan over
    2015, 2016, 2019 and 2020 gives no row for 2017 or 2018. A harvest stopped
    before its last cell covers only the cells it ran. Without a plan, or with
    one that sent no year limit, the years run from the first year in the
    records to the last. A year that holds records keeps its row in every case,
    and a set in which no record has a year gives an empty frame. The R twin's
    ``autoplot()`` counts a record set's years by the same rule.

    ``fill=False`` counts only the years that hold records, as earlier
    versions did.

    The records' ``attrs["retrieved_at"]`` is carried to the result, so
    :func:`scopusflow.plots.plot_trend` can say when the last year plotted was
    still being indexed.
    """
    years = pd.to_numeric(records["year"], errors="coerce").dropna()
    counts = {int(y): int(n) for y, n in years.astype(int).value_counts().items()}
    if fill and counts:
        span = _searched_years(records) or range(min(counts), max(counts) + 1)
        for year in span:
            counts.setdefault(int(year), 0)
    out = _trend_frame(counts)
    stamp = records.attrs.get("retrieved_at")
    if stamp is not None:
        out.attrs["retrieved_at"] = stamp
    return out

compare_topics(reference_query, comparison_terms, years, field=None, view='STANDARD', **kwargs)

Compare comparison topics against a reference topic over the years.

Each comparison query is (reference) AND (term), after field has wrapped each side. A reference containing OR or AND NOT therefore keeps its meaning, and every comparison set is a subset of the reference. The year limit is appended to each query as :func:scopusflow.count.scopus_count appends it.

Returns a :data:COMPARISON_COLUMNS frame. One count request per term per year, plus one per year for the reference topic, so keep the term and year counts modest to stay within quota.

Every count is sent with refresh=True unless you pass refresh. pybliometrics keys its own response cache on the query string and view alone, so without refresh=True a reference harvested earlier could be counted from the rows the harvest left there. The terms would still be counted by the API, and a share of the two could pass 100%. refresh=False, or a number of days, opts in to that cache, and a count it answers is warned about. The key ignores keyword filters such as subj, so fold any filter into the queries before you opt in.

Raises :class:scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowConfigError before any request when pybliometrics.init() has not been called in the session.

Source code in src/scopusflow/compare.py 
def compare_topics(reference_query: str, comparison_terms, years: Sequence[int],
                   field: str | None = None, view: str = "STANDARD",
                   **kwargs) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Compare comparison topics against a reference topic over the years.

    Each comparison query is ``(reference) AND (term)``, after ``field`` has
    wrapped each side. A reference containing OR or AND NOT therefore keeps its
    meaning, and every comparison set is a subset of the reference. The year
    limit is appended to each query as :func:`scopusflow.count.scopus_count`
    appends it.

    Returns a :data:`COMPARISON_COLUMNS` frame. One count request per term per
    year, plus one per year for the reference topic, so keep the term and year
    counts modest to stay within quota.

    Every count is sent with ``refresh=True`` unless you pass ``refresh``.
    pybliometrics keys its own response cache on the query string and view
    alone, so without ``refresh=True`` a reference harvested earlier could be
    counted from the rows the harvest left there. The terms would still be
    counted by the API, and a share of the two could pass 100%.
    ``refresh=False``, or a number of days, opts in to that cache, and a count
    it answers is warned about. The key ignores keyword filters such as
    ``subj``, so fold any filter into the queries before you opt in.

    Raises :class:`scopusflow.exceptions.ScopusFlowConfigError` before any
    request when ``pybliometrics.init()`` has not been called in the session.
    """
    if not reference_query or not str(reference_query).strip():
        raise ValueError("reference_query must be a non-empty string.")
    if isinstance(comparison_terms, str):
        comparison_terms = [comparison_terms]
    terms = [str(t).strip() for t in comparison_terms]
    if not terms or any(not t for t in terms):
        raise ValueError("comparison_terms must be a non-empty list of non-empty terms.")
    if years is None or not list(years):
        raise ValueError("years must be a non-empty sequence.")
    ys = sorted(set(_check_years(years)))
    # Every query is checked offline before the first request, so a bad term
    # cannot fail the comparison after the reference counts have been paid for.
    _check_query(str(reference_query).strip(), field)
    for term in terms:
        _check_query(term, field)
    kwargs.setdefault("refresh", True)
    require_init()

    from pybliometrics.scopus import ScopusSearch  # imported lazily; needs a key

    def size(query: str, year: int) -> int:
        full = _and_clause(query, f"PUBYEAR IS {year}")
        t0 = time.time()
        search = ScopusSearch(full, view=view, download=False, **kwargs)
        # stacklevel 3 reaches compare_topics' caller from inside size() on
        # Python 3.12 and later. Earlier versions give each comprehension that
        # calls size() a frame of its own (PEP 709), so there the warning names
        # this module.
        return result_size(search, t0, kwargs["refresh"], full, stacklevel=3)

    ref_query = wrap_field(str(reference_query).strip(), field)
    # One count step per term, plus the reference; logged as "Cell k/N:" so the
    # app's progress parser can drive a bar (mirrors the R verbose output).
    total = len(terms) + 1
    logger.info("Cell 1/%d: counting reference across %d year(s)", total, len(ys))
    ref_counts = {y: size(ref_query, y) for y in ys}

    comparison = []
    for i, term in enumerate(terms):
        logger.info("Cell %d/%d: counting '%s'", i + 2, total, term)
        # Both sides are bracketed, as in scopus_intersections(). Joined bare, an
        # AND NOT reference took the term into its negation, and the comparison
        # set outgrew the reference.
        cmp_query = f"({ref_query}) AND ({wrap_field(term, field)})"
        comparison.append((term, cmp_query, {y: size(cmp_query, y) for y in ys}))

    return _assemble(str(reference_query).strip(), ref_query, ref_counts, comparison, ys)

Type Description DataFrame

One row per concept and per intersection, with columns label, query, n (the count, as a nullable integer), type ("concept" or "intersection"), size (the number of member concepts) and members (the member labels, joined by "; "). The years restriction, when given, is stored in df.attrs["years"].

Notes

This performs one count request per concept and per intersection, so it needs a valid API key and internet access, exactly as :func:scopusflow.count.scopus_count does.

Further keyword arguments reach each of those counts, and so does its default of refresh=True. pybliometrics' own response cache, keyed on the query string and view alone, would otherwise answer a concept that an earlier harvest downloaded with the number of rows that harvest left there. refresh=False, or a number of days, opts in to that cache, and a count it answers is warned about. The key ignores keyword filters such as subj, so fold any filter into each concept's query before you opt in.

Source code in src/scopusflow/intersections.py 
def scopus_intersections(
    concepts: Mapping[str, str],
    intersections: Sequence[Sequence[str]] | None = None,
    abbrev: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    sep: str = " × ",
    years: Sequence[int] | None = None,
    field: str | None = None,
    view: str = "STANDARD",
    verbose: bool = False,
    **kwargs,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Count each concept and each requested intersection of concepts.

    Parameters
    ----------
    concepts:
        A mapping whose keys are display labels and whose values are search terms
        (wrapped in ``field`` when one is given) or complete field-tagged query
        expressions such as ``"TITLE(virtual reality)"`` (used as-is). The labels
        must be unique.
    intersections:
        An optional sequence of sequences, each naming two or more distinct
        concept labels whose intersection should be counted, for example
        ``[["A", "B"], ["A", "B", "C"]]``. A single flat sequence of labels is
        taken as one intersection.
    abbrev:
        An optional mapping of short labels, keyed by concept label and used only
        when composing intersection labels, so those rows stay readable while the
        concept rows keep their full names.
    sep:
        The separator joining member labels in an intersection label; defaults to
        a multiplication sign between spaces.
    years:
        Optional publication years, applied to every count as one inclusive
        range from the earliest year to the latest, as
        :func:`scopusflow.count.scopus_count` applies them, so ``[2015, 2020]``
        covers every year from 2015 to 2020.
    field:
        An optional Scopus field tag wrapped around each concept value that is not
        already a complete field-tagged expression (see
        :data:`scopusflow.query.FIELD_TAGS`).
    view:
        The Scopus search view, ``"STANDARD"`` or ``"COMPLETE"``.
    verbose:
        When ``True``, progress is reported on the ``scopusflow`` logger.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        One row per concept and per intersection, with columns ``label``,
        ``query``, ``n`` (the count, as a nullable integer), ``type``
        (``"concept"`` or ``"intersection"``), ``size`` (the number of member
        concepts) and ``members`` (the member labels, joined by ``"; "``). The
        ``years`` restriction, when given, is stored in ``df.attrs["years"]``.

    Notes
    -----
    This performs one count request per concept and per intersection, so it needs
    a valid API key and internet access, exactly as
    :func:`scopusflow.count.scopus_count` does.

    Further keyword arguments reach each of those counts, and so does its
    default of ``refresh=True``. pybliometrics' own response cache, keyed on the
    query string and view alone, would otherwise answer a concept that an
    earlier harvest downloaded with the number of rows that harvest left there.
    ``refresh=False``, or a number of days, opts in to that cache, and a count
    it answers is warned about. The key ignores keyword filters such as
    ``subj``, so fold any filter into each concept's query before you opt in.
    """
    out = _intersection_rows(concepts, intersections, abbrev, sep, field)

    ys = sorted(set(_check_years(years))) if years else None
    if verbose:
        n_inter = int((out["type"] == "intersection").sum())
        logger.info(
            "Counting %d queries (%d intersection%s).",
            len(out), n_inter, "" if n_inter == 1 else "s",
        )

    counts: list[int] = []
    for label, query in zip(out["label"], out["query"], strict=True):
        if verbose:
            logger.info("Counting %s", label)
        counts.append(scopus_count(query, years=ys, view=view, **kwargs))
    out["n"] = pd.array(counts, dtype="Int64")

    out = out[["label", "query", "n", "type", "size", "members"]]
    out.attrs["years"] = ys
    return out

plot_trend(trend, ax=None)

Plot publication counts over time as a filled area, line and points.

trend has columns ["year", "n"], as :func:scopusflow.trend.scopus_trend and :func:scopusflow.trend.year_counts return them. Returns the matplotlib Axes. An empty frame raises ValueError("The trend has no years to plot."), as the R twin's plot_scopus_trend() does.

When the years plotted reach the year recorded in trend.attrs["retrieved_at"], a note below the axis label says that the year was incomplete when the counts were taken, as in "2026 was incomplete when retrieved on 2026-09-29." Scopus goes on indexing a year's publications after the year has begun. The note is read from the recorded time alone, never from the clock of the session drawing the figure, so a trend that records none is drawn without it. The R twin's figures carry the same note in their caption.

def plot_trend(trend: pd.DataFrame, ax=None):
    """Plot publication counts over time as a filled area, line and points.

    ``trend`` has columns ``["year", "n"]``, as
    :func:`scopusflow.trend.scopus_trend` and
    :func:`scopusflow.trend.year_counts` return them. Returns the matplotlib
    ``Axes``. An empty frame raises
    ``ValueError("The trend has no years to plot.")``, as the R twin's
    ``plot_scopus_trend()`` does.

    When the years plotted reach the year recorded in
    ``trend.attrs["retrieved_at"]``, a note below the axis label says that the
    year was incomplete when the counts were taken, as in "2026 was incomplete
    when retrieved on 2026-09-29." Scopus goes on indexing a year's
    publications after the year has begun. The note is read from the recorded
    time alone, never from the clock of the session drawing the figure, so a
    trend that records none is drawn without it. The R twin's figures carry
    the same note in their caption.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    from .trend import _incomplete_note

    # An empty frame would otherwise fail inside numpy, or draw an empty axes.
    if len(trend) == 0:
        raise ValueError("The trend has no years to plot.")

    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots()

    years = trend["year"]
    counts = trend["n"]
    ax.fill_between(years, counts, alpha=0.16, color=_TREND_COLOUR)
    ax.plot(years, counts, color=_TREND_COLOUR, linewidth=2)
    ax.scatter(years, counts, color=_TREND_COLOUR, s=18, zorder=3)
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    ax.set_xlabel("Year")
    ax.set_ylabel("Records")
    note = _incomplete_note(years, trend.attrs.get("retrieved_at"))
    if note is not None:
        # Left-aligned with the axes and placed beneath the axis label, whose
        # drawn extent sets the height, so the note covers neither the label
        # nor the tick labels at any figure size.
        ax.annotate(
            note, xy=(0, 0), xycoords=("axes fraction", ax.xaxis.label),
            xytext=(0, -4), textcoords="offset points", ha="left", va="top",
            fontsize=7.5, color="#737373", annotation_clip=False,
        )
    _clean_axes(ax)
    return ax

def plot_top(top: pd.DataFrame, ax=None):
    """Plot a horizontal bar chart of the most frequent values, largest on top.

    ``top`` has columns ``["value", "n"]`` (from :func:`scopusflow.records.top`);
    each bar carries its count at its end, matching the R ``plot_scopus_top``.
    Returns the matplotlib ``Axes``.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    # An all-missing publication column tallies to no rows at all, which would
    # otherwise surface as an opaque max() error on the label widths below.
    if len(top) == 0:
        raise ValueError("The tally has no rows to plot.")

    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots()

    # Reverse so the largest count sits at the top of the chart.
    ordered = top.iloc[::-1]
    bars = ax.barh(ordered["value"].astype(str), ordered["n"], color=_TOP_COLOUR)
    labels = [f"{int(n):,}" for n in ordered["n"]]
    ax.bar_label(bars, labels=labels, padding=3, fontsize=8, color="#4d4d4d")
    # Headroom derived from the widest label, so the count on the longest bar
    # stays inside the axes, where a wide one would otherwise clip at the
    # right edge. Mirrors the
    # R plot's label-width-derived axis expansion.
    ax.margins(x=0.04 + 0.024 * max(len(lab) for lab in labels))
    ax.set_xlim(left=0)
    ax.set_xlabel("Records")
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    _clean_axes(ax)
    return ax

Plot each comparison topic's share of the reference literature over time.

comparison is the frame from :func:scopusflow.compare.compare_topics. With interval a shaded Wilson band shows how stable each yearly share is (illustrative, never a confidence interval, since Scopus counts are exact). highlight names one topic to draw in an accent colour, the rest in grey. With counts_in_legend (the default) each label carries the topic's total record count, for example machine learning (n = 1,204).

A legend is only drawn when there are too many topics to label the lines directly. legend_inside governs where it then sits: with the default False matplotlib chooses the least-obtrusive spot automatically (loc="best"); with True the legend is placed inside the axes, in whichever corner has the most free space, saving the width an outside legend would otherwise take. Returns the matplotlib Axes.
